title: NVIDIA Releases Alpamayo 2 Edge: A 2B Reasoning VLA for DRIVE Thor
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: NVIDIA has released Alpamayo 2 Edge , a compact reasoning vision-language-action (VLA) model for autonomous driving. Alpamayo 2 Edge is a 2B-parameter model that plans trajectories and explains them inside the vehicle. It targets NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor , not a datacenter GPU. The goal: reasoning-based planning within onboard compute and latency budgets. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR Size: 2B-class. Card breakdown: 2.45B backbone + 0.2B action expert (HF metadata says 3B). Context length: not disclosed (measured prompt: 3,236 tokens). Runs on: NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor with the FP8 + TensorRT Edge-LLM recipe. BF16 PyTorch needs 16 GB+ GPU memory, validated on 1x H100 80GB. Performance: Strong closed-loop driver for its size; mid-pack on reasoning QA. Best: 15.15 km per at-fault incident in AlpaSim, about 60x Qwen-Drive-1.0 4B (0.25 km). Worst: nuReasoning numeric score of 48.67; LingoQA 75.2 trails Alpamayo 2 Super (79.2). Bottom line: Best: reasoning-based planning at 160 to 190 ms on in-car hardware. Worst: only H100 validated, and real-time Thor speed needs the FP8 recipe. What is Alpamayo 2 Edge? Alpamayo 2 Edge is an open NVIDIA VLA model that turns surround-camera video into a 6.4-second plan. It is the in-car member of the Alpamayo family , next to the 34B cloud model Alpamayo 2 Super . Per the model card , the 2.45B backbone pairs a 1.96B language model with a 0.41B SigLIP2 encoder. A 0.2B diffusion action expert sits on top. The backbone comes from NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Edge and is Nemotron-based. NVIDIA markets the model as 2B, while Hugging Face metadata shows 3B. What goes in and what comes out? For trajectory prediction, the model reads 6 cameras and 22 frames per observation. The 2 front cameras give 5 frames each, the other 4 give 3 each. It also takes a navigation instruction and 20 historical ego poses. Output is 64 waypoints from 0.1 to 6.4 seconds. The action expert predicts acceleration and curvature, then a unicycle model integrates them. The text output is a Chain-of-Causation (CoC) reasoning trace. The model also answers free-form questions about a driving scene. How does adaptive reasoning work? During routine driving, the model emits special <NOMINAL> tokens instead of a full reasoning trace. It writes CoC reasoning only when a scene needs it. Fewer tokens means less c

summary.tldr:
NVIDIA has released Alpamayo 2 Edge, a 2B-parameter vision-language-action (VLA) model specifically engineered for the NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Thor platform. Designed for onboard autonomous driving, the model performs trajectory planning and scene explanation within strict latency constraints. It functions as the edge-deployed counterpart to the 34B-parameter Alpamayo 2 Super cloud model, utilizing a backbone derived from NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Edge and Nemotron architecture. The model is designed to process surround-camera video to generate a 6.4-second trajectory plan, outputting 64 waypoints alongside a Chain-of-Causation (CoC) reasoning trace.

Technically, the model architecture consists of a 2.45B backbone—comprising a 1.96B language model and a 0.41B SigLIP2 encoder—paired with a 0.2B diffusion-based action expert. Input data includes 6 camera feeds (22 frames total), navigation instructions, and 20 historical ego poses. For real-time in-car performance, the model requires an FP8 + TensorRT Edge-LLM recipe to achieve inference speeds of 160 to 190 ms on DRIVE AGX Thor hardware. While BF16 PyTorch execution has been validated on a single H100 80GB GPU, it requires over 16 GB of VRAM. The model employs adaptive reasoning, emitting special tokens during routine driving and reserving full CoC traces for complex scenarios to minimize token count and latency.

In performance benchmarks, Alpamayo 2 Edge achieved 15.15 km per at-fault incident in the AlpaSim environment, significantly outperforming Qwen-Drive-1.0 4B (0.25 km). However, it trails the larger Alpamayo 2 Super in LingoQA scores (75.2 vs 79.2) and recorded a nuReasoning numeric score of 48.67. While marketed as a 2B model, Hugging Face metadata indicates a 3B parameter count. The model is currently limited by its reliance on H100 validation for development, with real-time deployment contingent on the specific FP8 optimization recipe.
takeaways: **Architecture Composition:** 2.45B backbone (1.96B language model + 0.41B SigLIP2 encoder) plus a 0.2B diffusion action expert.
**Input/Output Specs:** Processes 6 cameras (22 frames), navigation instructions, and 20 ego poses to output 64 waypoints (0.1 to 6.4 seconds).
**Performance Metrics:** Achieved 15.15 km per at-fault incident in AlpaSim and a 75.2 score on LingoQA.
**Latency Targets:** Operates at 160 to 190 ms on DRIVE AGX Thor hardware using the FP8 + TensorRT Edge-LLM recipe.
**Adaptive Reasoning:** Emits special tokens for routine driving and full Chain-of-Causation traces only for complex scenes to reduce compute load.

title: Position-Skipped Distillation of Sparse-Attention Indexers: Train Short, Serve Long
author: Fu Dai
contentSnippet: Top-k sparse attention relies on an indexer, a lightweight per-layer module that ranks cached tokens so attention covers only the k highest-scoring ones. Indexers are usually distilled from dense attention at the full serving length, so every training step pays for long-context dense attention. We show that when an indexer is distilled on short sequences, its failure to generalise to longer contexts is driven mainly by rotary positional encoding (RoPE), not by degraded content matching. We propose position-skipped distillation: the indexer and the frozen teacher see short sequences whose position IDs contain a randomly placed gap, so neither ever processes more than the short training length. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Qwen3-30B-A3B, an indexer distilled on 8K tokens this way matches a 32K-distilled indexer to within about 0.5 perplexity up to 32K, and on DeepSeek-V2-Lite matches a 64K-distilled indexer at 64K with roughly 6x less training compute per token. On Llama-3.1-8B it trails the stronger 32K run by 0.6 perplexity, and at 64K simple position compression is often as good, so the main gain is training cost rather than quality. We also quantise indexer keys to 3-4 bits without retraining and score them with a fused integer kernel: at 4 bits, perplexity changes by at most 0.05 and the scan is 1.6-2.2x faster than half precision. In a current serving engine, the indexer speeds up decoding only for long contexts with multiple concurrent streams.

title: Why data centers are at the center of the Big Tech backlash
author: Anthony Ha
contentSnippet:
In his new book “Hyperscale,” journalist Paris Marx investigates the impact of data centers and generative AI, taking readers inside the data centers themselves and explaining how computing infrastructure that goes back decades recently became a political landmine.

The book is well-timed, to put it mildly, as data center backlash seems to have been one of the motivators for the massive blue wave seen in the recent midterm elections . And those debates are likely to continue as Democrats wield more governmental power .

In an interview with TechCrunch, Marx described the data center buildout as “fundamentally unsustainable” and “completely out of line with a livable planet,” while also arguing that these facilities make for an obvious target amidst broader anger at the tech industry. After all, if a data center is being built in your community, “it’s very physical, it’s very material.”

“It doesn’t matter what side of the political spectrum that you’re on,“ Marx said. “You are going to feel the effects of that in your quality of life, in your power bill, potentially in your access to water, potentially in what you hear around your community, if these air conditioning units on the roofs of data centers are making a lot of noise.”

He also suggested that data center opposition is only the most visible piece of a wider movement targeting “the physical manifestations of the tech industry, […] whether it’s the opposition to Flock cameras rolling out across the United States, or the smart glasses that Meta is trying to put on people’s faces, or even the self-driving cars that Waymo is rolling out.”

During our conversation (which I’ve edited for length and clarity), Marx and I discussed data centers’ environmental impact, how tech companies are responding to community resistance, and what it’s actually like inside a data center.

Getting inside of a hyperscale data center was not the easiest task in the world. I spoke to some researchers who have been doing research on data centers for a number of years longer than I had, and they told me that before the generative AI moment, and before all the a

summary.tldr:
In his book 'Hyperscale,' journalist Paris Marx examines the environmental and social impact of the global data center buildout, framing the infrastructure as a 'fundamentally unsustainable' manifestation of Big Tech’s expansionist ambitions. Marx argues that the physical presence of these facilities—which consume vast quantities of electricity and water—has turned them into political flashpoints, citing community resistance in regions like Chile, Ireland, and Oregon as evidence of a growing backlash against the tech industry's resource demands.

Technically, Marx describes the modern hyperscale data center as a highly securitized, utilitarian environment characterized by extreme noise levels from cooling fans and strict access controls requiring passport verification and key-card authentication for every internal door. The book highlights specific instances of resource strain, such as data centers consuming over 20% of Ireland’s electricity, leading to a 2022 grid connection moratorium in Dublin, and Google’s usage of 29% of the water supply in The Dalles, Oregon. Marx contends that the current trajectory of AI-driven infrastructure expansion is disconnected from tangible societal benefits, prioritizing corporate power over local community stability and environmental sustainability.
takeaways: **Ireland Grid Impact:** Data centers in Ireland consume over 20% of the country's total electricity, prompting a 2022 moratorium on new grid connections in the Dublin area.
**Oregon Water Usage:** Google’s data center operations in The Dalles, Oregon, were revealed to account for 29% of the city's total water consumption.

**Security Protocols:** Access to modern hyperscale facilities requires advance passport submission and multi-layered physical security, including key-card access for every individual door within the facility.

**Operational Environment:** Server rooms are described as utilitarian, high-temperature environments with extreme noise levels generated by cooling fans, necessitating hearing protection for extended stays.

**Community Resistance:** Opposition to data centers is categorized by Marx as part of a broader movement against the physical manifestations of Big Tech, including Flock cameras, Meta smart glasses, and Waymo autonomous vehicles.

title: Binding of Isaac developer removes AI music from Repentance Plus
author: Terrence O’Brien
contentSnippet: The Binding of Isaac: Repentance Plus has spent the last few days getting review-bombed on Steam after it was discovered that a particular segment of the game used AI music. Reddit user ShweetsStuff discovered the songs used during a Grand Theft Auto-themed section. They found several audio files with Suno metadata that pointed back to the tracks on Suno’s site. Creator Edmund McMillen took to X to apologize and claimed he “had no idea” the in-game GTA parody used generative AI music. Adding to the drama, Valve requires developers to disclose how and when they use generative AI in the development process, and Nicalis, Inc., the studio behind Repentance Plus, doesn’t appear to have mentioned the AI music anywhere. [Media: https://twitter.com/edmundmcmillen/status/2124169167880470745?s=20] Within hours of the discovery, Nicalis shared on X that Repentance Plus had been updated and the generated music files had been removed. While reviews on Steam have yet to rebound, and the game is still rated as “overwhelmingly negative,” users on X seem to be giving McMillen the benefit of the doubt, likely because he’s been quite outspoken on AI in game development, calling it “uninspired and bland” in a TikTok from 2024. [Media: https://twitter.com/nicalis/status/2124241453266169887]

summary.tldr:
The Binding of Isaac: Repentance Plus faced significant community backlash and Steam review-bombing following the discovery of AI-generated music within a Grand Theft Auto-themed segment of the game. Reddit user ShweetsStuff identified the tracks by locating Suno metadata embedded in the audio files, which linked directly to the Suno platform. This discovery triggered immediate scrutiny regarding compliance with Valve’s mandatory disclosure policies for generative AI usage in software development, which the publisher, Nicalis, Inc., reportedly failed to satisfy.

Creator Edmund McMillen publicly apologized on X, stating he was unaware that generative AI had been utilized in the game's development. McMillen has previously expressed public disdain for AI in game design, characterizing it as "uninspired and bland" in a 2024 TikTok. In response to the controversy, Nicalis, Inc. issued an update to remove the AI-generated audio files within hours of the initial discovery. Despite the removal, the game’s Steam rating remains "overwhelmingly negative" as of the latest reports.
takeaways: **Discovery Method:** Reddit user ShweetsStuff identified the AI music by finding Suno metadata embedded within the game's audio files.
**Regulatory Compliance:** The publisher, Nicalis, Inc., failed to disclose the use of generative AI to Valve, violating Steam's mandatory disclosure requirements for AI-integrated software.
**Remediation:** Nicalis, Inc. released an update to remove the AI-generated tracks within hours of the public discovery.
**Creator Stance:** Edmund McMillen, the game's creator, publicly disavowed the use of AI, citing his previously stated belief that such tools produce "uninspired and bland" content.

title: The vibe-coding revolution is coming to all the gadgets
author: David Pierce
contentSnippet: This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on the vibe-hacking of everything, follow David Pierce. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here. How it started Like so many things with AI, it’s not that large language models opened up some wholly new capability. For as long as there have been gadgets, a few users have been hacking, modding, jailbreaking, and tweaking them to their liking. What is new is that it’s easy now. People all over the world are discovering that they can use large language models to hack their hardware simply by prompting Claude Code or Codex to do it. It has led to a boom in developer-friendly gadgets and created a market for better software on just about every device you can think of. For one developer in India who goes by Gathin T, the whole thing started almost on a whim. “One afternoon, I was fiddling with my TV, and it was just really shitty,” he tells me. His was a set made by Xiaomi and running Android TV, with so many ads and so much interface chaos it was hard to even change inputs. And he got to thinking: If you can install another launcher on your Android phone, maybe you can do the same to your TV. “The first thing that came to mind was to remove the bloatware from the TV,” he says. “Then I thought, why not make it look better?” Gathin prompted Claude Code and discovered that with a couple of permissions tweaks and a toggle of USB debugging mode, his chatbot could control his TV as long as they were on the same Wi-Fi network. An hour and a half later, Gathin had redesigned his TV to his liking — no more onscreen ads, a simpler interface, easier access to his PlayStation on another input. He posted on X about what he’d done and promptly went viral. So Gathin put together his work, bought a domain, and launched CleanYourTV as a tool for helping other people solve their own television interfaces. It became one of the most popular repositories on GitHub, got thousands of pull requests and feature ideas, and inspired countless people to point their own chatbot at their big screen. Gathin is careful to note that the only TVs that work this easily are based on Android. (He has Claude Code-d his way through other operating systems, but those involve more explicit jailbreaking and rooting, so he’s more reluctant to

summary.tldr:
The rise of 'vibe-coding'—using LLMs like Claude Code and Codex to reverse-engineer, modify, and jailbreak consumer hardware—is transforming the landscape of device customization. Developers and non-technical users are increasingly leveraging AI to bypass bloatware, unlock hidden APIs, and repackage firmware for devices ranging from Android-based TVs and cameras to synthesizers and gaming consoles. A notable example is the 'CleanYourTV' project, which allows users to strip ads and simplify interfaces on Xiaomi Android TVs by automating USB debugging and permission tweaks via LLM-generated scripts.

This trend has triggered a defensive response from manufacturers, particularly in the gaming sector, where companies are moving toward more invasive DRM and cloud-streaming architectures to prevent decompilation. Industry experts like former Take-Two AI head Luke Dicken suggest this will lead to a broader industry shift toward platform-level lockdowns. Conversely, some manufacturers are embracing the trend; for instance, M-Vave released open-source firmware for its FM-1 synthesizer to accommodate the hacker community. Meanwhile, the hardware ecosystem is shifting toward modular, developer-friendly platforms like ESP32 modules (e.g., M5Stack PaperMono), which are increasingly being used to build bespoke, single-purpose consumer devices, a movement Meta is currently supporting through its Muse Gadgets program.
takeaways: **CleanYourTV Methodology:** Uses LLMs to automate the removal of bloatware and interface customization on Android-based TVs by toggling USB debugging and modifying system permissions.
**Gaming Industry Response:** Executives anticipate a shift toward more invasive DRM and streaming-only models to mitigate the risks of AI-assisted decompilation and unauthorized platform porting.
**Hardware Shift:** The community is increasingly favoring ESP32-based modules over traditional jailbreaking, as these platforms are designed for custom firmware and modular functionality.
**Corporate Adoption:** Meta is actively entering the space with its 'Muse Gadgets' program, providing a pathway for users to deploy custom AI-driven software on ESP32 hardware.

**Risk Profile:** Vibe-coding carries significant bricking risks, leading developers like Gathin T to implement automated backup and verification agents within their tools to mitigate potential system failures.

title: Best Personal AI Agents in 2026: OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, Gemini Spark and More, Compared on Memory, Security and Cost
author: Asif Razzaq
contentSnippet: A personal AI agent runs continuously, keeps memory across sessions, and acts inside your apps. You talk to it in a chat app, by email or by voice. It keeps working after you close the window. The category started small. OpenClaw began in November 2025 as Clawdbot, a weekend project by Peter Steinberger. Twelve months later, Google, OpenAI, Meta and Perplexity all ship their own versions. The products split into 2 camps. Self-hosted agents run on your machine or server and use any model you choose. Managed agents run on a vendor’s cloud VM and come bundled with a subscription. How we ranked them We scored each agent on 3 axes that matter once an agent holds your inbox and credentials. Memory: what persists, where it is stored, and whether you can read, edit or delete it. Security: default permissions, the isolation boundary, approval gates, and the public incident record. Cost: the subscription price, or token spend plus hosting for self-hosted options. Facts come from vendor documentation, launch posts and independent security research. Prices are US list prices as of November 21, 2026. Ranking reflects overall fit for an individual user, not raw capability. title: SAE-Audit: Clinical-Trial Prediction via Inference-Time Optimization of Black-Box LLMs Audited by Sparse Autoencoder Evidence
author: Junbo Shen
contentSnippet: Clinical trials are costly and often take years to complete, making early outcome prediction valuable for trial planning. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to forecast clinical-trial outcomes, yet their predictions remain unreliable and their rationales may not faithfully reflect the evidence underlying their answers. On tasks such as predicting whether a registered clinical trial will complete or terminate early, frontier LLMs perform only modestly above chance in our experiments. We introduce SAE-Audit, which optimizes a black-box LLM at inference time with evidence obtained from a deployable open model. A frozen sparse autoencoder (SAE) on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct is converted into a vocabulary of clinical concepts. Sparse probes fitted on past trials determine which concepts are associated with the outcome. For a new protocol, the concepts detected by the probe are written as evidence, each with the direction and strength of its association with the outcome, and the LLM being audited optimizes its answer in the light of this evidence. Without additional training, SAE-Audit raises balanced accuracy of deepseek-v4-flash by 9.6--12.0 points on five clinical-trial prediction tasks and raises GPT-5.6-terra by 8.0 points on trial completion, exceeding other agentic inference-time optimization methods by a large margin. As an auxiliary, SAE probes module within SAE-Audit is itself accurate and auditable, providing natural-language explanations directly derived from verified concept contributions and protocol evidence, without requiring additional LLMs at inference time. SAE-Audit provides verifiable, concept-level evidence for more accurate and auditable clinical-trial prediction. It can also be embedded into biomedical AI agents such as Biomni to optimize their performance.

title: Google AI Previews Tool Retrieval in the Gemini API for Large Tool Libraries
author: Michal Sutter
contentSnippet: Google has launched Tool Retrieval in the Gemini API , now in preview in the Interactions API. Gemini API Tool Retrieval lets an agent keep a large tool library available. It does not send every parameter schema in every prompt. The model loads a schema only when a task needs that tool. For agents wired to dozens of functions or MCP servers, it targets a real cost: tool definitions. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR Tool: An API feature with no stated tool cap. Google advises static loading under 20 stable tools. Runs on: Google’s servers (server-side search) or your own registry (client-side). Interactions API, v1beta only. Performance: Search, schema load and function call resolve in 1 API request in server mode. Best: 0 extra round trips and no index to host for server-side retrieval. What is Gemini API Tool Retrieval? Tool Retrieval is a Gemini API feature that defers tool parameter schemas until the model asks for them. Google’s documentation states the problem plainly. A few dozen function declarations can consume tens of thousands of tokens on every request. With deferral, the model sees only each tool’s name and a short description. It does not see the parameter schema until retrieval. How does defer_loading work in the Gemini Interactions API? You add {"type": "tool_search"} to the tools array. Then you set defer_loading: true on each function to hold back. The @googledevs launch post shows a deferred issue_refund function on gemini-4-hydrogen . Its code comment mentions 50+ other deferred functions. When the model needs a deferred tool, the response contains 3 steps: tool_search_call : the model requests a tool by name. tool_search_result : the API returns the full schema. function_call : the model emits the call your code executes. The API resolves the first 2 steps itself. Your app only runs the function_call and returns a function_result . Deferred functions can carry an optional short_description . It is shown during retrieval and is valid only when defer_loading is true. Server-side vs client-side retrieval Server-side is the default. Gemini runs the search, so there is no index to build or host. Client-side mode uses "execution": "client" . Your app runs its own lookup, such as an embedding index, registry or permission filter. It returns matching declarations in functi

summary.tldr:
Google has introduced 'Tool Retrieval' for the Gemini API, currently in preview within the Interactions API (v1beta). This feature addresses the token overhead associated with large tool libraries by deferring the loading of parameter schemas until the model specifically requests them. By only providing the tool name and a short description in the initial prompt, developers can avoid consuming tens of thousands of tokens per request, which is a common bottleneck when managing dozens of functions or MCP servers.

Technically, the implementation involves setting 'defer_loading: true' on functions and adding '{"type": "tool_search"}' to the tools array. The process operates in three steps: the model emits a 'tool_search_call', the API returns the full schema via 'tool_search_result', and finally, the model emits the 'function_call'. In server-side mode, the API handles the search, schema load, and function call resolution within a single API request, eliminating extra round trips. For more complex requirements, a client-side mode allows developers to manage their own lookup logic, such as embedding indices or permission filters, by setting 'execution: "client"'.
takeaways: **Token Efficiency:** Prevents large tool libraries from consuming excessive tokens by hiding parameter schemas until the model explicitly requires them.
**Implementation:** Requires adding '{"type": "tool_search"}' to the tools array and setting 'defer_loading: true' on individual function declarations.
**Deployment Modes:** Supports server-side retrieval (default, no index hosting required) and client-side retrieval (custom lookup logic via 'execution: "client"').
**Usage Recommendation:** Google advises static loading for scenarios involving fewer than 20 stable tools, while Tool Retrieval is intended for larger, dynamic libraries.
**API Workflow:** The API automatically resolves the search and schema retrieval steps, leaving the developer to handle only the final 'function_call' and 'function_result'.

title: WAFT: A Fourier-Analytic Framework for Steady-State Performance of Walker Constellations
author: Haoyang Xue
contentSnippet: The Walker configuration is predominantly adopted by nongeostationary orbit constellations exemplified by Starlink and Kuiper. The steady-state distribution of aggregate downlink interference power is critical for spectrum coexistence regulation. Large-scale time-stepped simulation and stochastic geometry (SG)-based models are the mainstream methods for obtaining the distribution, but are either computationally expensive or subject to inherent bias. This paper models the aggregate downlink interference power as an additive observable and proposes the Walker-constellation Analysis via Fourier Transform (WAFT) framework to derive the steady-state performance. Modeling the constellation as a periodic impulse array on the phase torus, the spectral representation of the observable is derived via 2-D Fourier analysis. Analytical expressions for the expectation, variance, and steady-state complementary cumulative distribution function are further derived, and the periodicity of receiver performance along longitude is characterized. For a Starlink sub-constellation example, numerical validation shows that the percentile discrepancies of WAFT relative to a finite-duration time-stepped simulation remain within 0.09~dB. Comparisons with isotropic and intensity-matched SG models reveal that the conditional independence of satellite positions alone makes the models assign a substantial probability mass to physically infeasible values, producing percentile discrepancies.

title: Edit-Induced Dependency Mismatch: Propagation Omissions, Recovery, and Evaluation Blind Spots in Coding Agents
author: Fei Ding
contentSnippet: During iterative code modification, coding agents may continue to rely in subsequent reasoning on outdated dependency judgments whose text remains fixed in the context, leading to errors in subsequent reasoning and leaving consumer defects undetected by the original task evaluations, thereby exposing blind spots in the tested benchmarks. We study actual agent execution trajectories collected on benchmark tasks: deepseek-v4-flash runs on DeepSWE and SWE-bench Verified, supplemented by Qwen3.8-Flash cases on FeatureBench. Focusing on edit-induced consumer obligations, a full-corpus blinded human audit of the DeepSWE runs identifies terminal mismatches, including diagnoses whose task scope remains disputed. Following supplementary execution checks, all retained DeepSWE terminal events have execution support. The audit also shows that recovery within a trajectory can coexist with terminal omissions in the same run. The process analysis links the presentation of relevant consumer code to explicit dependency judgments and subsequent synchronization actions recorded in the trajectories. An explicit dependency-review prompt reduces terminal omissions under the tested conditions, supporting re-derivation of consumer obligations after edits. Local replays of selected DeepSWE cases show that synchronizing the diagnosed consumers restores the target behavior while the listed controls continue to pass. Cross-benchmark execution counterexamples show that the original task evaluations do not fully detect edit-induced dependency mismatches: patches pass those evaluations, yet additional execution checks confirm unintended defects along existing consumer paths. These findings support measuring task scores, terminal propagation states, and recovery separately.

title: Meta ads is now available in AWS Quick
author: Chris Geiger
contentSnippet: Marketers have never had more data to act on. Take an apparel brand that advertises on Meta technologies: campaign results live in Meta Ads Manager, briefs and creative assets in shared storage, and inventory, customer lifetime value, and in-store purchases in a data lake. Analysts export reports, merge spreadsheets, and rebuild the same deck each week, and the data ages before anyone acts on it. When the team does decide what to change, someone returns to Ads Manager to update campaigns, ad sets, budgets, and audiences by hand. As a result, teams judge campaigns on metrics alone, and the path from insight to action stays slow and manual. Today, AWS Quick added a Meta ads AI connector. The connector gives Quick access to ads Model Context Protocol (MCP) server operations. Meta ads customers can use natural language to create, manage, and analyze campaigns within Quick, while staying connected to the Meta ad management network. Marketers can complete tasks with support from AI, such as pulling insights to understand ads performance, creating product catalogs, and editing existing or creating new campaigns. Quick can also combine Meta ad management data with first- and third-party data sources to create dashboards, documents, slide decks, and automated workflows. “Meta ads AI connector through Quick gives our marketing teams one place to go from campaign planning to execution. It lets us act on business insights directly in our ads, without the handoffs and tool switching that slow campaigns down. With fal.ai’s image, audio, and video models in the same workflow, we’ll test more creative ideas and spend more time reaching customers.” — Tina Sang, Head of Marketing at fal.ai Demo: Meta ads in Quick The video shows how to install the Meta ads connector from Customize > Connectors in AWS Quick, sign in with Facebook, and choose which Pages, Businesses, and Instagram accounts AWS Quick can access. The other builds a dashboard comparing spend, leads, and cost per lead for two ad sets, with recommended tests to run next. summary.tldr:
AWS Quick has integrated a new Meta ads AI connector, enabling marketers to manage, analyze, and execute advertising campaigns directly within the Quick interface. This integration aims to eliminate manual data exports and tool switching by centralizing campaign planning, execution, and reporting within a single workflow.

title: A Team of Researchers from Columbia and CertiK Introduce TensorLean for Formal Verification of GPU Kernels
author: Michal Sutter
contentSnippet: Researchers from Columbia University and CertiK have introduced TensorLean , a framework for formal verification of GPU kernels at the PTX level. TensorLean is a Lean-based verifier that proves compiled kernels match a tensor-level math spec. The research team checked 149 kernel instances , including every kernel of FlashAttention-2, -3 and -4 plus DeepGEMM. It proved 83 correct. The remaining 66 led to 38 correctness bugs. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension . TL;DR Size: 1.8K-line PTX parser. Specs total 10,278 lines against 151,285 lines of kernel source, a ratio near 15:1. Runs on: A 16-core workstation. It checks PTX compiled for A100, H100 and B200 kernels. Performance: 83 of 149 kernel instances proved correct, 38 bugs found across 6 projects. Best: Caught a FlashAttention-4 data race that never appeared in 17,760 test runs. What is TensorLean? TensorLean is a formal verification framework for GPU kernels at the PTX level. It starts from unmodified source code. A developer writes a tensor-level spec in Lean. TensorLean then proves 4 properties: no data races, termination, correct output within tolerance, and untouched memory elsewhere. How does TensorLean verify a GPU kernel? Specs build on Lean’s Mathlib. Tensor operators follow PyTorch names, so @ means torch.matmul . Each spec has 5 parts: spec_math , spec_mut , spec_layout , spec_tol and requires . The math stays separate from the memory layout. The pipeline runs in 7 steps: Start from unmodified source. Write the tensor-level spec. Compile to PTX and load a PTX semantics. Build a happens-before graph to check races and termination. Symbolically execute to get final memory, identical across schedules. Lower the spec to PTX-memory level. Discharge proofs with Lean’s kernel, Z3 and cvc5. Which techniques make it scale? Concurrency to sequential: Race-freedom proofs on the happens-before graph cover all CTAs, threads and loop iterations symbolically. Loop invariants over semirings: Closed forms for tiled, accumulating loops, such as online softmax, need 1 SMT query per loop. Tolerance proofs: Algebraic error is proved zero. Round-off error is bounded separately, then combined. Assertions as hints: Developers add tensorlean_assert in source. Each is proved once, then reused. What bugs did TensorLean find? The GitHub README lists 38 bugs,

summary.tldr:
Researchers from Columbia University and CertiK have unveiled TensorLean, a formal verification framework designed to validate GPU kernels at the PTX (Parallel Thread Execution) level. By utilizing the Lean theorem prover, the framework verifies that compiled kernels align with high-level tensor math specifications. The system operates on unmodified source code, requiring developers to write tensor-level specifications that define four core properties: absence of data races, guaranteed termination, output correctness within specified tolerances, and memory safety (ensuring no unintended memory modification).

In a comprehensive evaluation, the team applied TensorLean to 149 kernel instances across six projects, including FlashAttention-2, -3, and -4, as well as DeepGEMM. The framework successfully proved 83 instances correct while identifying 38 distinct correctness bugs. Notably, TensorLean detected a data race in FlashAttention-4 that had remained hidden through 17,760 standard test runs. The verification pipeline involves a 1.8K-line PTX parser and utilizes Lean’s Mathlib, Z3, and cvc5 to discharge proofs. The system supports kernels compiled for NVIDIA A100, H100, and B200 architectures and maintains a specification-to-source code ratio of approximately 1:15, with 10,278 lines of specifications covering 151,285 lines of kernel source.
takeaways: **Verification Scope:** TensorLean proved 83 out of 149 kernel instances correct and identified 38 bugs across projects including FlashAttention, Liger Kernel, TileOPs, TileLang, and DeepGEMM.

**Technical Architecture:** The framework uses a 7-step pipeline that includes building a happens-before graph for race detection, symbolic execution, and discharging proofs via Lean’s kernel, Z3, and cvc5.

**Scalability Techniques:** The system employs symbolic race-freedom proofs across all CTAs and threads, uses loop invariants over semirings for tiled loops, and separates algebraic error proofs from round-off error bounds.
**Hardware Support:** The framework is compatible with kernels compiled for NVIDIA A100, H100, and B200 GPUs and runs on standard 16-core workstation hardware.

**Specification Structure:** Each specification consists of five components: spec_math, spec_mut, spec_layout, spec_tol, and requires, allowing for the separation of mathematical logic from memory layout.

title: Handover Cost Optimization in LEO Satellite Networks using an RL-based Multiple-Column Selection Strategy via Branch-and-Price
author: Mandar R. Nalavade
contentSnippet: Next-generation wireless networks increasingly rely on low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites for broad coverage and low latency, making efficient handover management essential. We formulate satellite handover as a combinatorial optimization problem, assigning each ground user to exactly one capacity-limited, visible satellite while minimizing network handover costs. We propose a reinforcement learning (RL)-based branch-and-price (B&P) framework with learned multiple-column selection (MCS) to accelerate column generation while retaining exact dynamic programming pricing. We also develop two lightweight heuristic policies: handover-aware visibility duration (HAVD) for online decisions and congestion-aware predictive (CAP) for offline planning. Additionally, a local-search repair algorithm adapts precomputed B&P or MCS-B&P solutions to demand perturbations through single-flip and per-user trajectory re-optimization, avoiding complete re-optimization. Simulations using realistic large scale constellations, including Starlink Gen-1, demonstrate that MCS-B&P achieves solution quality comparable to exact B&P with fewer column-generation iterations, fewer branch-and-bound nodes, and reduced computation time. HAVD and CAP offer effective online and offline cost-latency trade-offs, while local-search repair recovers most performance losses due to demand perturbations at a fraction of the computational cost of full re-optimization.

title: When Can a Rewiring Control Test LLM Weight Readers? C2 and an Eligibility Protocol
author: Vaishak Girish Kumar
contentSnippet: Large language models can predict the outputs of small neural networks from raw weights, but success could reflect recognition of weight-space regularities (fingerprints) rather than computation, and function-preserving controls cannot tell these apart. We propose C2, a counterfactual that permutes the columns of a network's final linear readout: every other parameter, and the readout's singular values, norms and entry multiset, are unchanged, and the function can change in an exactly recomputable way; we verify that each evaluated permutation does. C2 separates fingerprinting from computation only under three conditions, which we state as an eligibility protocol: a strategy restricted to C2-invariant summaries must already predict the target; C2 must change a property specific to the rewiring; and the reader's identity must be attested. No natural setting we tested is eligible. On tiny MLPs a frontier reader route followed the rewired function on all 24 networks, but invariant baselines were near chance and its backend could not be attested. In two public CNN zoos the conditions traded off: weight statistics predicted CIFAR-10 accuracy in-distribution, but C2's effect on accuracy was not specific to the swap, while per-image targets were specific but not predictable from invariant summaries. On a constructed population where a planted fingerprint rule works, all conditions hold and C2 separates a rule-following reader from an executor. A self-hosted Qwen3.8-27B followed the rewired function rather than the shortcut, and showed no evidence of using the weights with thinking disabled. A registered replication on fresh networks confirmed both findings (tracking minus stuck 0.875, 95% interval [0.750, 1.000]), and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B also followed the rewiring (tracking minus stuck 0.729 [0.552, 0.885]). The transforms, audits and raw records are available from the authors.

title: From Footprints to Service Regions: Modeling and Analysis of Dense LEO Satellite Networks Using an Orbit-Aware Cox Point Process
author: Chang-Sik Choi
contentSnippet: In dense low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite networks, several accessible satellites cover the same location. A footprint therefore identifies where communication is feasible but does not determine which satellite serves each user. The service region of a satellite, namely the set of locations it serves, governs satellite load, resource sharing, and user throughput. Using an orbit-aware Cox point process on a common orbital shell, we model each service region as the intersection of a satellite's spherical-cap footprint and its spherical Voronoi cell under nearest-satellite association. We then use Palm calculus to derive exact expressions for the mean area and perimeter and a coverage--load identity. After coverage saturates, mean area and load decrease inversely with population. In contrast, adding satellites along existing orbits leaves a positive limiting mean perimeter. We connect this geometry to an approximate noise-limited user rate. Along the tested densification paths, the increase in user rate comes mainly from the decrease in mean satellite load rather than from the improvement of the serving link. We also compare the model with Walker constellations with Starlink-type parameters, using Cox parameters matched to the local orbit and satellite densities at each latitude. The model reproduces the mean area and perimeter of these constellations over broad latitude ranges, with larger differences near component maximum latitudes. These results show that service-region geometry, and hence satellite load and user rate, depend not only on the total satellite population but also on its allocation across orbital planes.
