title: Three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of the Dell Technologies New York Symposium
author: Victoria Gayton
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 19:21 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026

Three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of the Dell Technologies New York Symposium

AI operational readiness requires more than selecting the right servers, storage and computing capacity.

Those considerations are particularly consequential for financial institutions , where reliability, regulatory obligations and the need to demonstrate returns on technology investments shape deployment decisions. Meanwhile, AI is changing the threat landscape, giving less sophisticated attackers access to capabilities that once required considerably greater resources, according to John Scimone , president and chief security officer of Dell Technologies Inc.

“I think the pyramid still exists, but undoubtedly, the cost of entry and the barriers to entry have crumbled,” he told theCUBE . “Said another way, the least sophisticated attack tomorrow is more sophisticated than the world will have ever seen a year ago.”

Scimone spoke with theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante during the Dell Technologies New York Symposium , part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exclusive coverage on theCUBE. Across the event , Dell executives and cloud infrastructure providers examined the economics of enterprise AI, the operational challenges of scaling infrastructure and the decisions shaping AI adoption.

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with John Scimone:

Here are three insights you might have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of the Dell Technologies New York Symposium:

Insight #1: Enterprise AI requires a new operating and economic model.

Dell has spent nearly two years running fully autonomous agents internally, capturing institutional knowledge in machine-readable skill files that guide their behavior. The effort is part of a broader reorganization of work around AI agents, according to John Roese , global chief technology officer and chief AI officer of Dell.

“It doesn’t mean you can’t use frontier models and open models,” he said during the event . “It just means that when you design your AI system, you need to realize that the thing that is your moat is not the actual tools. It’s not even the models. It’s the special knowledge that’s now manifesting in these new forms that really capture what you know and do differently than your competitors.”

Here is theCUBE’s complete video discussion with John Roese:

The financial side of A

summary.tldr:
At the Dell Technologies New York Symposium, Dell executives and industry partners detailed the evolving operational and economic requirements for enterprise AI. Dell CTO John Roese revealed that the company has spent nearly two years developing autonomous agents internally, utilizing machine-readable skill files to capture institutional knowledge, which he identifies as the primary competitive moat rather than the underlying models themselves. CFO David Kennedy emphasized that financial readiness now requires shifting from variable token consumption models to more predictable, efficient usage patterns, often by leveraging open-weight models for repetitive financial tasks to control costs.

Infrastructure strategy is shifting toward a distributed model spanning data centers, cloud environments, and the edge to manage rising inference costs. Dell SVP Kyle Dufresne noted that organizations are increasingly pushing inference to the edge to maintain performance and cost-efficiency. Simultaneously, supply chain constraints for AI-critical components—including processors, memory, and rack-level cooling—are causing project delays of 60 to 120 days, prompting Dell to urge earlier collaborative planning with clients. Security remains a critical concern, with Dell CSO John Scimone warning that the barrier to entry for sophisticated cyberattacks has collapsed, rendering even "least sophisticated" future attacks more dangerous than historical precedents.
takeaways: **Internal AI Strategy:** Dell has spent two years building autonomous agents that utilize machine-readable skill files to codify institutional knowledge.
**Supply Chain Delays:** Demand for AI server components like cooling, networking, and processors is currently causing project lead-time delays of 60 to 120 days.
**Market Access:** Comet Cloud Inc. is targeting small-to-medium businesses excluded by major cloud providers' multiyear contract requirements by offering isolated, dedicated compute clusters.

**Sovereign Infrastructure:** Alpha Compute Corp. is utilizing Dell and Intel hardware to build "sovereign-by-design" neocloud enclaves, focusing on data residency and confidential computing requirements.

**Security Landscape:** Dell CSO John Scimone reports that the cost and technical barriers to entry for cyberattacks have significantly decreased, increasing the threat level for all enterprise deployments.

title: Cut self-hosted LLM cost and latency with the distributed KV caching agent skill
author: Ravi Yadav
contentSnippet: Customers increasingly self-host large language models (LLMs) on GPUs for control over cost, accuracy, and latency. However, self-hosting often means paying for redundant GPU work because small, isolated caches on each server can’t hold or share the growing context AI agents and chat applications resend. Consider a legal AI assistant that can accumulate hundreds of thousands of tokens of case history in each conversation. When a lawyer returns to a thread after lunch, responses from the LLM can take minutes. The GPU server that picks up the request has none of that history in its memory. So, the GPU recomputes the key-value (KV) attention states for all of those tokens, a step called prefill, before it writes a word. The same pattern slows down resumed coding agents, agentic AI assistants, and document Q&A assistants. Distributed KV caching with Amazon ElastiCache can cut self-hosted LLM inference costs by up to 40% and time to first token (TTFT) by up to 80%. Distributed KV caching extends GPU-local caches with a shared tier beside your GPU fleet so any server can reuse KV state for days across sessions, routing shifts, and server failures. “ Announcing distributed KV caching for self-hosted LLMs with Amazon ElastiCache ” dives into the technical details and the performance benchmarks. This post details the distributed KV caching skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS. With this skill, you can evaluate and set up distributed KV caching from within your coding agent in a few prompts. The skill guides the agent through checking whether your workload benefits from distributed KV caching, setting up a cache cluster for testing or production workload, and troubleshooting your LLM inference caching. The skill works with Kiro , Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and other coding agents that support Agent Skills. We walk through how the skill works with four conversations: diagnosing a slow first token, sizing and pricing the cache, setting it up, and fixing a failed transfer. Why a skill for KV caching and what can it do? The benefits for your workload depend on characteristics such as LLM models used, user traffic patterns, and prompt routing choices, and can be complex to estimate. We created the KVTrace tool to get close estimates of the benefits for your workload, from your own model and traffic before you deploy any infrastructure, at no additional charge. The skill simp

summary.tldr:
Amazon has introduced a distributed KV caching architecture for self-hosted LLMs using Amazon ElastiCache, designed to mitigate the latency and cost overheads associated with redundant prefill computations. By offloading key-value (KV) attention states to a shared, external cache tier, the system allows GPU fleets to retrieve existing context across different sessions, routing shifts, or server failures. This approach specifically targets long-context applications like legal assistants or coding agents, where recomputing hundreds of thousands of tokens results in significant time-to-first-token (TTFT) delays.

AWS claims this distributed caching strategy can reduce self-hosted LLM inference costs by up to 40% and improve TTFT by up to 80%. To facilitate adoption, AWS released a dedicated 'distributed KV caching skill' within the Agent Toolkit for AWS, which enables coding agents—including Kiro, Claude Code, and OpenAI Codex—to automate the evaluation, cluster setup, and troubleshooting of the caching infrastructure. Additionally, AWS provides a tool called KVTrace, which allows users to estimate potential performance gains and cost savings based on their specific model, traffic patterns, and prompt routing before deploying any infrastructure.
takeaways: **Performance Metrics:** Distributed KV caching can reduce time-to-first-token (TTFT) by up to 80% and lower self-hosted LLM inference costs by up to 40%.
**Tooling Integration:** The distributed KV caching skill is part of the Agent Toolkit for AWS and is compatible with coding agents such as Kiro, Claude Code, and OpenAI Codex.
**Estimation Tool:** The KVTrace tool is provided at no additional charge to simulate workload benefits and infrastructure requirements before deployment.
**Core Functionality:** The architecture extends GPU-local caches with a shared tier via Amazon ElastiCache, enabling persistence of KV states across sessions and server failures.

title: Self-WSP: Can Language Models Improve Themselves Through Weight-Space Programming?
author: Guoming Ling, Shanshan Zhong, Kaixuan Zhang, Zhongzhan Huang
contentSnippet: Frontier language models can now read and edit the weights of a neural network much like code and thereby improve a small model, an approach known as Weight-Space Programming (WSP). We further explore applying WSP to a language model itself, which we call Self-WSP. Specifically, Qwen3.5-0.8B reads its own weights, proposes an edit, and then continues with the edited weights as both problem solver and editor. We find many cases of genuine self-improvement. Self-edits can raise GSM8K accuracy from 11.8% to 62.2% and MATH500 accuracy from 7.0% to 32.2%, sometimes by changing only 16 parameters, and in some cases repeated self-editing keeps improving the model. A closer look, however, reveals that these gains lack interpretability. The model shows little understanding of the edits it makes, and WSP driven by random search sometimes performs comparably. Self-WSP thus holds promise as a path toward recursive self-improvement (RSI), but realizing this promise requires further exploration.

title: How Google Duplex evolved to also call businesses for you in Gemini
author: Google AI Research Blog
contentSnippet:
November 20, 2026 Yossi Matias, Vice President, Google & GM, Google Research, Yaniv Leviathan, Google Fellow, Google Research, and Janet Zhou, Group Product Manager, Google Maps

When we introduced Google Duplex in 2018, it pioneered natural voice conversations between AI and local businesses over the phone. Since then, this technology has worked behind the scenes across many Google products. These capabilities are integrated directly in Tasks in Gemini .

Completing tasks like making dinner reservations or booking a hair appointment is time consuming. Live phone conversations move fast and rarely follow a script. The person on the other end can say almost anything, often revising their thoughts mid-sentence – and people often rely on subtle tone changes to indicate whose turn it is to speak. Pause half a second too long, and it sounds like the call dropped; speak too soon, and you end up talking over each other. Leveraging AI to complete these tasks respectfully over the phone required us to consider high quality speech understanding, contextual reasoning, and speech synthesis working together in a single, low-latency system.

We introduced Google Duplex nearly a decade ago to help address this challenge. Propelled by advances in foundation models, the Duplex architecture has evolved to power autonomous task completion across many core products, such as Google Search and Maps. This week, we launched Duplex in Tasks in Gemini App , a personal AI collaborator that can help coordinate real-world chores, like calling businesses for you and handling real-world requests on behalf of the user. In this post, we look back at the decade-long architectural evolution that made this possible — moving from early, closed-domain models to a unified stack built entirely with Gemini.

From closed-domain calls to Tasks in Gemini

What began as a narrow, task-specific system quickly expanded into a shared conversational infrastructure, built in collaboration with teams across Google.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, when business hours and services shifted rapidly, Duplex doubled down on verifying merchant info automatically to keep listings accurate. It remains an important data source; for example, business information sourced from Duplex’s phone calls had been shown in Search and Maps over one trillion times , as we shared in 2023.

Simultaneously, we worked with Android and

summary.tldr:
Google has officially integrated its decade-old Duplex technology into 'Tasks in Gemini,' enabling the AI to autonomously place phone calls to businesses on behalf of users. This launch marks the culmination of a ten-year architectural evolution, transitioning from narrow, task-specific recurrent neural networks to a unified stack powered entirely by Gemini. The system is designed to handle real-world complexities such as scheduling appointments, checking service availability, and managing multi-constraint requests like coordinating car maintenance around existing calendar conflicts.

The technical architecture has progressed through three distinct eras: initial closed-domain models trained on specific task flows; a hybrid phase (circa 2022) using LaMDA paired with deterministic state-tracking guardrails; and the current Gemini-based system. The modern stack utilizes free-text prompting to generalize across business categories without requiring bespoke dialogue models. To address the challenges of live telephony, Google employs custom acoustic models for sub-second latency in noisy environments and pragmatic grounding to interpret social cues, such as polite indirect refusals or conversational pauses, ensuring natural interaction cadence.
takeaways: **Architectural Evolution:** The system moved from pre-transformer recurrent neural networks to a hybrid LaMDA-based stack, and finally to a unified Gemini-powered architecture capable of handling unbounded tasks.
**Operational Scale:** Data gathered via Duplex phone calls has been surfaced in Google Search and Maps over one trillion times as of 2023.
**Latency Optimization:** The stack utilizes custom acoustic and conversation cadence models to maintain sub-second response times despite background noise like kitchen clatter or street traffic.
**Business Controls:** Merchants can opt out of automated calls via Google Business Profile settings or by verbally requesting the AI to stop during a call.
**Deployment History:** The technology has been integrated into five generations of Pixel devices via 'Call Screen' and 'Hold for Me' features since 2019.

title: Introducing managed cluster extensions for observability and user management in Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Slurm
author: Austin Cherian
contentSnippet: Keeping a shared Slurm cluster for foundation model development in sync entails keeping several separately maintained pieces of configuration matched to what’s running on the nodes. The cluster’s shape lives on multiple configuration files, its software in custom scripts, its network topology in files that must be edited as nodes change, and its users in a roster that an administrator must maintain and rerun. Over time these pieces drift away from what’s actually running, and nothing tells you when they do. We believe cluster configurations should be managed the way you manage the rest of your AWS infrastructure. You declare what you want through an API or the console, AWS validates it before it’s applied, the cluster is kept in that state continuously, and you can see whether it’s working. During 2026, Amazon SageMaker HyperPod brought that approach to Slurm clusters, with API-driven Slurm configuration, AMI-based configuration, continuous provisioning, automatic topology management, and deep health checks. Today, we launched cluster extensions, which bring the same approach to the software and settings on running nodes, with managed extensions for observability and user management. However, through all of it, you still keep full access to every node in your cluster, including the controller node. You can SSH in, configure nodes directly, and run your own lifecycle scripts. The APIs give you less to maintain, direct access gives you more control, and you choose the balance. In this post, we walk through the features we introduced in 2026 and explain why the software on running nodes needed a different mechanism. We then show how cluster extensions work, through both the API and the console, and follow a platform team through a quarter on a cluster that uses them. A declarative foundation for Slurm cluster operations We can think of a Slurm cluster’s configuration grouped into six layers. Five of them describe the cluster itself: its definition, node setup, capacity, network topology, and hardware health. The sixth covers the software running on its nodes, which we discuss in the next section. Figure 1: The Slurm cluster configuration stack Earlier in 2026, we brought declarative management to the first five layers. With API-driven Slurm configuration , administrators define node roles, partitions, and Amazon FSx for Lustre and Amazon FSx for OpenZFS mounts

summary.tldr:
Amazon has introduced managed cluster extensions for SageMaker HyperPod Slurm, extending declarative infrastructure management to the software and settings layer of running nodes. This update builds upon the 2026 rollout of API-driven Slurm configuration, which previously automated node roles, partitions, and storage mounts for Amazon FSx for Lustre and OpenZFS. The new extensions specifically target observability and user management, aiming to eliminate configuration drift that occurs when cluster state deviates from manual configuration files, scripts, and network topology definitions.

The system categorizes Slurm cluster configuration into six distinct layers: cluster definition, node setup, capacity, network topology, hardware health, and node-level software. While the first five layers were addressed earlier in 2026 through continuous provisioning and automatic topology management, the software layer required a new mechanism to handle the dynamic nature of running nodes. Despite the shift toward API-driven, declarative management, Amazon maintains full user access, allowing administrators to SSH into controller nodes, execute custom lifecycle scripts, and perform direct manual configurations alongside the managed extensions.
takeaways: **Configuration Layers:** Amazon defines Slurm cluster operations across six layers: cluster definition, node setup, capacity, network topology, hardware health, and node-level software.
**Managed Extensions:** New functionality specifically automates observability and user management tasks on running nodes to prevent configuration drift.
**Declarative Management:** The system allows administrators to define desired states via API or AWS Console, with AWS performing validation and continuous state enforcement.
**Administrative Access:** Users retain full root-level access to all nodes, including the controller node, for manual configuration and custom script execution.
**2026 Infrastructure Rollout:** Previous HyperPod Slurm updates included API-driven configuration, AMI-based setup, continuous provisioning, automatic topology management, and deep health checks.

title: Introducing Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Global Inference Gateway: One endpoint across Regions and clusters
author: Dmitry Soldatkin
contentSnippet: During a traffic peak, a request can sit in a queue on a saturated HyperPod cluster while GPUs on another cluster, sometimes in another AWS Region, sit idle. You have already paid for that capacity, but your requests can’t reach it. In Introducing Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Inference Gateway , we showed how the Inference Gateway gives each Amazon SageMaker HyperPod cluster a single, GPU-aware endpoint. It reads real-time signals such as key-value (KV) cache utilization and queue depth to place every request on the best-suited pod. That solves routing inside one cluster, but not across clusters. Today, SageMaker HyperPod introduces the Global Inference Gateway. It is one SageMaker-managed gateway that routes across every cluster you register, in one Region or across Regions. The gateway picks the cluster and carries the request over the AWS backbone, with automatic failover and authentication through AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4) and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). Inside each cluster, the Inference Gateway keeps picking the pod, unchanged. The Global Inference Gateway is the second tier of the architecture we described in part 1. The challenge: Capacity spread across clusters and Regions Models are getting larger, and the GPU capacity to serve them is harder to find. To get enough of it, you spread it across more clusters and more Regions. Consider a team that serves four models across five HyperPod clusters in two Regions. Without the Inference Gateway, clients track 20 endpoints: one per model per cluster. The Inference Gateway cuts that to five, one per cluster. But each client still picks a cluster itself. That choice has costs: Uneven load. During peaks, requests queue in one Region while GPUs in the other Region are idle. Manual failover. When a cluster fails, an engineer changes configuration to move traffic away from it. Custom plumbing. Spreading traffic across Regions means building and maintaining load balancers, DNS, and cross-Region networking yourself. The team needs one endpoint that sends each request to the best-suited cluster and moves traffic off a failed cluster on its own. Key benefits The Global Inference Gateway helps you get more from the GPU capacity you already have, with less to operate. Put idle GPUs to work. During a peak, requests overflow to clusters with available capacity in the same Region or another one, instead

summary.tldr:
Amazon has introduced the SageMaker HyperPod Global Inference Gateway, a managed service designed to unify GPU inference across multiple clusters and AWS Regions. By providing a single endpoint for registered clusters, the gateway eliminates the need for clients to manage individual endpoints for every model-cluster combination. It utilizes real-time telemetry, including KV cache utilization and queue depth, to dynamically route traffic to the most suitable cluster, effectively addressing the issue of idle GPU capacity during localized traffic spikes.

The architecture functions as a second tier to the existing local Inference Gateway, which handles pod-level routing within a single cluster. The Global Inference Gateway operates over the AWS backbone, incorporating automatic failover capabilities and security via AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4) and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM). This system removes the operational burden of manual load balancing, custom DNS configuration, and cross-Region networking, allowing organizations to treat geographically dispersed GPU resources as a single, cohesive pool.
takeaways: **Routing Logic:** Uses real-time signals like KV cache utilization and queue depth to place requests on the optimal cluster.
**Security Integration:** Authenticates traffic using AWS Signature Version 4 (SigV4) and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM).
**Operational Efficiency:** Replaces the need for managing individual endpoints per model per cluster, reducing complexity for multi-Region deployments.
**Resiliency:** Features automatic failover to redirect traffic away from unhealthy clusters without manual configuration changes.

title: Anthropic researcher claims to have proven Riemann hypothesis using Claude
author: Maria Deutscher
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 16:28 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026

Anthropic researcher claims to have proven Riemann hypothesis using Claude

An Anthropic PBC researcher claims to have used Claude to prove the Riemann hypothesis, which is widely considered to be the most important open question in mathematics.

Levent Alpöge announced his discovery today on his personal website. Anthropic has not published an official announcement about the news. The company floated on the Nasdaq a day earlier in a landmark public offering that raised over $93 billion.

“I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis,” Alpöge wrote in a four-page statement. “What I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.”

The Riemann hypothesis was proposed in the mid-1800s by its namesake, the mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It focuses on a specific mathematical function, the Riemann zeta function, that was discovered more than a century earlier. A function is similar to a software program: It takes a piece of data as input and outputs another piece of data. A function’s input and output can be numbers, other functions and many other mathematical objects.

The Riemann zeta function’s input and output are both complex numbers. Complex numbers share similarities with regular numbers, but also have many additional properties. When the inputs and outputs of the Riemann zeta function are visualized, they resemble a three-dimensional spiral.

The Riemann hypothesis is concerned with a specific section of that 3D spiral. In that section, the complex numbers outputted by the Riemann zeta function all equal zero. The hypothesis argues that the inputs from which those outputs are derived all include the value ½.

The hypothesis is considered to be the most important open problem in mathematics for multiple reasons. The first is that although it focuses on a single, not overly complicated mathematical function, its implications extend to a far bigger topic: prime numbers. If the Riemann hypothesis is correct, a seemingly random aspect of prime numbers is in fact regulated by a pattern.

Another factor behind the hypothesis’ importance is that hundreds of theorems operate on the assumption that it’s true. If the Riemann hypothesis is correct, those theorems are correct as well.

Alpöge wrote that Claude proved not o

summary.tldr:
Levent Alpöge, a researcher at Anthropic, has claimed to have proven the Riemann hypothesis—a foundational open problem in mathematics concerning the distribution of prime numbers—using the company's Claude AI model. The announcement follows Anthropic's recent Nasdaq IPO, which raised over $93 billion. Alpöge asserts that the proof covers both the standard Riemann hypothesis and its generalized variant, suggesting that the model is capable of addressing even broader mathematical conjectures in the future.

The proof is reportedly massive, spanning over 250,000 pages, and has not yet been released in full. However, Alpöge has published a machine-verifiable version of the proof written in Lean, a programming language designed for formal mathematical verification. The Lean implementation consists of millions of lines of code; because Lean proofs function as software programs, the argument is considered verified if the code executes without error. The Riemann hypothesis itself posits that all non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function have a real part equal to ½, a discovery that would validate hundreds of dependent mathematical theorems.
takeaways: **Proof Scale:** The generated proof document exceeds 250,000 pages in length.
**Verification Method:** A formal version of the proof has been implemented in the Lean programming language, consisting of millions of lines of code.
**Scope of Discovery:** The claim includes a proof for both the standard Riemann hypothesis and the generalized Riemann hypothesis.
**Corporate Context:** The announcement occurred one day after Anthropic's Nasdaq IPO, which raised more than $93 billion.

title: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.
author: Dan Goodin
contentSnippet: Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve. The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model. Update, Nov 21: Posts on both Hacker News and X report that OpenRouter has sent customers an email notifying them that some of their prompts may have been read. OpenRouter cited the research and said that it received a report that the potential exposure involved prompts sent to MiniMax, a China-based model provider. OpenRouter said the researchers' planted URLs were accessed whether the prompts were sent to MiniMax directly or through three other resellers: AtlasCloud, Novita, and StreamLake. OpenRouter has removed a "Zero Data Retention" label from MiniMax-model endpoints. Hat tip: Sulat.com . Read full article Comments

summary.tldr: HD Moore, Chief Research Officer at Dragos, conducted a large-scale security audit of the AI inference supply chain by injecting 2 million unique 'canary' secrets—including AWS access keys, SSH passwords, and private repository URLs—into prompts sent across various AI routers, resellers, and hosting providers. The experiment revealed that sensitive data is frequently exposed, logged, and exfiltrated at multiple hops within the inference stack, as prompts are decrypted at each intermediary node to facilitate routing and model selection decisions.
takeaways: **Compromised Providers:** Attackers successfully siphoned credentials from three separate hosting providers, using stolen AWS keys 'tens of thousands' of times to probe S3 buckets, secrets managers, and AWS Bedrock configurations.

**Front-Door Exfiltration:** Evidence suggests attackers compromised providers at the 'front door' of the inference stack, as some keys were stolen even when the provider rejected the request before model execution.

**Privacy Flag Failure:** Multiple providers ignored 'Zero Data Retention' (ZDR) and 'no data collection' flags, with one unnamed Chinese AI lab scraping secret URLs from two-thirds of prompts explicitly marked for no data retention.

**Reseller Logging:** Several inference resellers were identified as malicious actors that log user prompts to harvest credentials, confirmed by Moore through A/B testing requests across different sellers for the same underlying model.
**Data Flow Leakage:** Prompts sent to US-based hosting providers were found to flow back to foreign labs, effectively bypassing geographic data residency expectations for customers.

title: How Standard Bank Group automates AI risk assessment for generative AI
author: Tala Qraitem
contentSnippet: This post is co-written with Tala Qraitem from AWS and Jörg Fischer from Standard Bank Group Having an AI policy is one thing. Proving, one use case at a time, that AI systems follow it is another. Every new generative AI application adds one more system to prove. Teams can now build one in days, but each still needs a risk committee’s approval before it reaches customers or employees. When that approval depends on reviewers reading documents and testing the system by hand, governance becomes the slowest step in the pipeline. Standard Bank Group chose to automate that proof. Working with AWS Professional Services, the bank deployed an automated assessment that scores each generative AI use case against international AI standards and its own policies. The assessment produces reports and a dashboard that show what is already in place, what is working well, and what still needs mitigation. This post explains how the assessment runs on AWS and what Standard Bank Group learned from its first runs. Governing AI with the framework you already have Standard Bank Group didn’t need a new AI policy. Like most large banks, it already had an established model risk practice that covers concerns such as explainability and fairness, and a change risk process that assesses each new use case according to its level of risk before it goes live. Generative AI increases the complexity, because models and tooling change every three to six months, yet each use case still needs to meet the same high security and compliance bar. “At Standard Bank, this assessment demonstrates how we are working with AWS to embed intelligent, automated risk management into our AI journey, allowing us to accelerate meaningful business value while maintaining the trust and controls that banking demands. We believe responsible AI is not about slowing innovation down but enabling it to build and scale with confidence.” — Jörg Fischer, Group Chief Information and AI Officer, Standard Bank Group The goal was to automate evidence gathering and testing, then feed the results into the approval gates Standard Bank Group already runs. Review and approval stay with the risk committee, but the committee now bases each decision on consistent evidence, collected the same way across use cases. How the assessment works Figure 1 shows how the assessment’s components fit together in Standard Bank Group’s AWS account, fr

summary.tldr:
Standard Bank Group, in collaboration with AWS Professional Services, has implemented an automated AI risk assessment framework to streamline the governance of generative AI applications. By integrating automated evidence gathering and testing into existing model risk and change risk processes, the bank aims to reduce the manual review burden that typically delays deployment. The system evaluates each generative AI use case against both international AI standards and the bank’s internal compliance policies, generating standardized reports and dashboards that provide risk committees with consistent data for decision-making.

The architecture leverages the bank's existing AWS environment to address the rapid evolution of generative AI models and tooling, which typically update every three to six months. Rather than replacing the human-led risk committee, the automated framework serves as a prerequisite for approval, ensuring that all applications meet the bank's security and compliance requirements before reaching customers or employees. According to Jörg Fischer, Group Chief Information and AI Officer at Standard Bank Group, this approach is designed to accelerate the scaling of AI initiatives while maintaining institutional trust and control.
takeaways: **Governance Integration:** The system maps generative AI assessments directly into Standard Bank Group’s pre-existing model risk and change risk management frameworks.
**Operational Goal:** The primary objective is to replace manual document review and hand-testing with automated evidence collection to accelerate the approval pipeline.
**Technical Scope:** The framework produces centralized dashboards and reports that highlight existing controls, performance metrics, and required risk mitigations for each use case.
**Strategic Rationale:** The bank identified that the rapid 3-to-6-month release cycle of AI models and tools necessitates automated compliance to prevent governance from becoming a bottleneck.

title: Announcing Amazon Textract Insights: Verifiable generative AI for documents
author: Keith Mascarenhas
contentSnippet: Organizations across financial services, insurance, healthcare, and the public sector depend on document processing. They turn scanned files and paper forms into structured data their systems can act on. As generative AI has matured, these organizations want more than accurate text extraction. They want to describe the information they need in their own words and get dependable, auditable answers from complex documents. Today, we are announcing the general availability of Amazon Textract Insights , a new generative AI feature of Amazon Textract available through a new API within Amazon Textract. With Amazon Textract Insights, you describe the fields you want in natural language and submit a document or a mixed, multi-document packet. You receive structured results in which each value carries a confidence score and page-level grounding, with no model training required. The challenge of extracting data from mixed packets Many of the high-value document workloads involve diverse, mixed packets rather than clean, single-purpose files. A mortgage file, for example, typically arrives as a single scan holding a W-2, payslips, bank statements, and a page of handwritten notes. Each has its own layout and appears in no fixed order. Claims files and onboarding packages can look very similar: typed forms, dense tables, scanned receipts, and free-text letters interleaved in one file. Teams usually take one of two approaches, and each has trade-offs. The first is a custom pipeline that combines optical character recognition, document splitting, classification, a foundation model prompt, and a review step. The team must integrate, scale, and operate all of it. The second is a general-purpose large language model used by default. It returns fluent answers but does not reliably cite the source page or give a confidence score. Without a traceable source and a calibrated score, it is hard to know which values to accept automatically and which to review. This uncertainty often limits how far teams can automate. Amazon Textract Insights is built for reliable document processing, bringing this entire workflow into a single asynchronous request on Amazon Textract. Rather than assembling and operating a custom pipeline, your team works through one managed API and moves directly to the data it needs. How Amazon Textract Insights works With Amazon Textract Insights, you define what t

summary.tldr:
Amazon has announced the general availability of Amazon Textract Insights, a generative AI feature integrated directly into the Amazon Textract API. Designed for document-heavy sectors like finance, insurance, and healthcare, the service allows users to extract structured data from complex, mixed-document packets—such as mortgage files containing interleaved W-2s, payslips, and handwritten notes—using natural language descriptions. The system eliminates the need for custom pipelines that combine OCR, document classification, and foundation model prompting, instead providing a single asynchronous API request that returns structured results.

Technically, Amazon Textract Insights differentiates itself from general-purpose LLMs by providing verifiable output. Every extracted value is accompanied by a confidence score and page-level grounding, allowing organizations to automate data ingestion with higher auditability. By moving the entire workflow into a managed service, Amazon aims to solve the 'black box' problem of standard LLMs, which often lack source citations and calibrated confidence metrics, thereby enabling higher levels of automated processing without requiring additional model training.
takeaways: **Service Integration:** Amazon Textract Insights is now generally available as a new API feature within the existing Amazon Textract service.
**Core Capability:** Users can extract specific fields from mixed, multi-document packets using natural language prompts without performing custom model training.
**Verifiability:** Each extracted data point includes a confidence score and page-level grounding to ensure auditability and source traceability.
**Workflow Efficiency:** The service replaces multi-step custom pipelines (OCR, splitting, classification, and LLM prompting) with a single asynchronous API request.

title: Daniel Ek backs AI researcher’s fusion power startup. Here’s what they’re building.
author: Tim De Chant
contentSnippet:
Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a stealthy fusion power startup founded by an AI researcher who is taking a different approach to developing a fusion power plant.

The U.K.-based startup was founded in February, though sources told TechCrunch that the founder, Nantas Nardelli, has been working on the idea for longer. The people asked not to be identified because the information isn’t public. Bloomberg first reported Ek’s backing of Europa Fusion.

Nardelli has extensive experience in the AI world, having previously worked at Google DeepMind, Facebook AI Research, and Microsoft Research Cambridge. Recently, he was head of machine learning at Pacific Fusion , the fusion power startup based in Fremont, California.

Pacific Fusion recently broke ground on a demonstration facility in New Mexico. Like most fusion startups of its size , Pacific Fusion leans heavily on physical devices to test its theories and improve its simulations.

Nardelli apparently didn’t agree with the focus on hardware, instead thinking that fusion startups should invest in a more simulation- and data-heavy approach, a source familiar with his thinking told TechCrunch.

Like Pacific Fusion, Europa Fusion will pursue a pulsed-power approach to fusion. Pulsed-power reactors use massive, perfectly timed surges of electrical current to compress fuel targets until the atoms inside fuse and release energy.

Fusion power has the potential to be a significant energy source in the coming decades, but to date, no one has built a power plant capable of supplying electricity to the grid. If fusion power becomes commercially viable, though, it could possibly be a significant source of carbon-free power that draws on nearly limitless fuel supplies. The technology also has the potential to alleviate concerns about AI’s energy consumption.

Fusion’s ability to generate electricity without exacerbating climate change apparently drove Nardelli’s pivot from AI.

“My original background is in electronics and control engineering,” he wrote on his website . “I used to build robots for a living. One day I’ll be back to that, but it’s time to fix climate change for good.”

Topics AI , Climate , Exclusive , fusion power , Startups When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . This doesn’t affect our editorial independence.

Tim De Chant is a senior climate rep

summary.tldr:
Spotify founder Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a U.K.-based fusion power startup founded in February by Nantas Nardelli. Nardelli, a former AI researcher with tenures at Google DeepMind, Facebook AI Research, and Microsoft Research Cambridge, previously served as the head of machine learning at Pacific Fusion. The startup aims to differentiate itself from competitors by prioritizing a simulation- and data-heavy development methodology over the hardware-centric approach common in the current fusion sector.

Europa Fusion intends to utilize a pulsed-power reactor architecture, which involves using precisely timed electrical current surges to compress fuel targets to induce fusion. This approach mirrors the technical strategy of Pacific Fusion, but Nardelli’s pivot from AI to fusion is predicated on the belief that advanced computational modeling can accelerate the path to commercial viability. The company's mission is to develop a carbon-free energy source capable of supplying the grid, potentially addressing the high energy demands of AI infrastructure.
takeaways: **Founder Background:** Nantas Nardelli is a former researcher at Google DeepMind, Facebook AI Research, and Microsoft Research Cambridge, and was formerly the head of machine learning at Pacific Fusion.
**Technical Strategy:** Europa Fusion focuses on a simulation- and data-heavy development model, diverging from the hardware-first approach used by many existing fusion startups.
**Reactor Architecture:** The company is pursuing a pulsed-power approach, which uses massive, timed electrical surges to compress fuel targets to trigger fusion.
**Funding:** The startup has secured backing from Spotify founder Daniel Ek.

title: AI claimed a solution to the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis — and a human did, too
author: Tim Fernholz
contentSnippet:
It’s a big week for Levent Alpöge: The mathematician saw his employer, Anthropic, become the first publicly traded frontier AI lab. He also appears to have solved one of the most important problems in mathematics.

“The precise timing is horrible,” he wrote in an essay announcing his findings and describing how he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last Sunday night to ask how to announce that he had found a Lean-compilable solution to the Riemann hypothesis, which dates back to 1859 and is among the Millennium Prize math problems.

The hypothesis conjectures that there is a hidden structure underlying the appearance of prime numbers. If the claimed result holds true, we’re entering sublime-mysteries-of-the-universe territory.

Maybe the best way to understand how exciting this is to the mathematics community is to watch the experts puzzling through the result in a chat on Zulip . Mathematicians like Chris Birkbeck, a number theorist at the University of East Anglia, are posting thoughts like this …

The cohomology bound is proved by what looks like an automorphy-lifting argument. It genuinely uses the existence of Galois representations attached to regular algebraic, polarized cuspidal automorphic representations of GL_n over CM fields, along with base change, Jacquet–Shalika, Clozel’s purity, Bernstein–Zelevinsky, the main theorem of CM, Deligne–Ribet and more.

For my part, I tapped out of mathematics at college calculus, so I can’t help decode exactly what that means.

But that comment was followed by 20 readers reacting 🤯.

It will be a while before the mathematics community feels like it has a handle on the proof, but most appear confident that the formalized Lean result will hold. Lean is an an open-source coding language used to express mathematical ideas as code, allowing proofs to be formally verified. Several participants in the Zulip chat, including MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland, say they have successfully confirmed that Alpöge’s solution can be compiled successfully.

Alpöge appeared in his essay to feel a bit guilty about releasing the proof without a truly human-intelligible explanation, but his obsession with the problem since childhood made him feel he “could not live” if he waited to release the finding.

Alpöge described a “stream-of-consciousness jaunt through the experience of finding all the pieces of the argument through incred

summary.tldr:
Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, has released a proof for the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis, a Millennium Prize problem concerning the distribution of prime numbers. Alpöge utilized Anthropic’s Claude model to assist in the derivation, describing the process as a stream-of-consciousness collaboration. The proof has been formalized in Lean, an open-source language for formal verification, and has been successfully compiled and verified by independent mathematicians, including MIT’s Andrew Sutherland. Alpöge also released a separate proof regarding the Navier-Stokes equations in collaboration with NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster.

Simultaneously, Stanford postdoc Alessandro Masullo has released a human-authored proof of the General Riemann hypothesis. Unlike Alpöge’s work, Masullo’s proof has not yet been expressed in Lean, and its validity remains subject to peer review. Stanford professor and American Mathematics Association president Ravi Vakil noted that Masullo’s work is the result of 12 years of independent research. The mathematical community is currently evaluating both submissions, with experts like Chris Birkbeck noting that Alpöge’s proof relies on complex techniques including automorphy-lifting arguments, Galois representations, and base change theorems.
takeaways: **Alpöge Proof Verification:** The Lean-formalized proof of the Riemann hypothesis by Levent Alpöge has been independently compiled and verified by multiple mathematicians.

**Technical Methodology:** Alpöge’s proof utilizes advanced number theory frameworks, specifically Galois representations attached to regular algebraic, polarized cuspidal automorphic representations of GL_n over CM fields.
**Competing Claim:** Stanford postdoc Alessandro Masullo released a separate, non-AI-assisted proof of the General Riemann hypothesis, which is currently undergoing community review.
**Additional Research:** Alpöge and NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster concurrently released a proof related to the Navier-Stokes equations.
**Institutional Context:** The article identifies Anthropic as a publicly traded frontier AI lab, noting significant equity stakes held by Amazon and Google.

title: AI deals shrink to as little as 30 days as the data layer sets the pace
author: Kelly Knight
contentSnippet:
UPDATED 14:27 EST / NOVEMBER 20 2026

AI deals shrink to as little as 30 days as the data layer sets the pace

Artificial intelligence has turned data infrastructure from a back-office purchase into the bottleneck that decides how fast GPUs pay off. As hyperscalers, neoclouds and enterprises race to expand their data layers, the way that infrastructure gets bought is changing just as fast.

The storage industry’s longtime performance specialist sees that shift as its opening. DataDirect Networks Inc. built its reputation on scale and speed, and those traits now carry more weight in AI infrastructure , according to Kevin Delane (pictured), president and chief revenue officer of DDN.

“When you look at the data layer, performance in the data layer drives value. So yes, it has to be simple, it has to be reliable. Those are table stakes, but performance drives business value,” Delane said.

Delane spoke with theCUBE Research’s Rebecca Knight and John Furrier at SC26 , during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how AI infrastructure sales cycles have grown more complex and faster, DDN’s tighter ecosystem work with partners such as Nvidia Corp. and Super Micro Computer Inc., and the company’s hiring for a direct, results-driven culture. (* Disclosure below.)

Faster, more complex AI deals reshape the data layer

The way companies buy AI infrastructure has changed along with the technology. Deals at neocloud providers no longer go to a single enterprise buyer. They now involve the off-taker renting the capacity, the cloud operator and the integration software layer, Delane explained. Timelines have shrunk just as sharply, from six months to a year for a traditional enterprise sale to as little as 30 days.

“The sales cycle is more complex for sure. The speed is insane,” Delane said. “Sometimes these things are 30 days and you have to be ready to turn things around and really work with your customers and partners quickly.”

DDN is answering with tighter ecosystem work. Its decade-long partnership with Nvidia anchors the strategy, and joint offerings with Super Micro , such as the Enterprise AI HyperPOD, aim to replace a data center buildout with a ready-to-run AI stack. At SC26, DDN also introduced software-defined EXAScaler deployment to give enterprise AI customers more choice of hardware.

“It takes the com

summary.tldr:
DataDirect Networks (DDN) President and CRO Kevin Delane reported at SC26 that AI infrastructure sales cycles have compressed significantly, dropping from traditional 6-12 month windows to as little as 30 days. This acceleration is driven by the critical role of the data layer in maximizing GPU utilization, where performance bottlenecks directly impact the return on investment for hyperscalers and enterprise AI deployments. DDN is responding to this market pressure by shifting its hiring focus toward technical and implementation staff rather than traditional sales roles, aiming to support rapid, results-driven deployments.

To address the complexity of modern AI infrastructure, DDN is deepening its ecosystem integration with partners like Nvidia and Super Micro Computer. Key offerings include the Enterprise AI HyperPOD, designed to replace custom data center buildouts with a pre-configured, ready-to-run stack that can be operational in approximately three hours. Additionally, DDN has introduced a software-defined version of its EXAScaler deployment to increase hardware flexibility for enterprise customers. Performance benchmarks cited by Delane for DDN’s Managed Lustre service on Google Cloud indicate a 70% improvement in training performance and a 40% increase in overall GPU efficiency.
takeaways: **Sales Cycle Compression:** AI infrastructure procurement timelines have shrunk from 6-12 months to as little as 30 days due to the urgency of GPU utilization.
**Deployment Speed:** The DDN and Super Micro Enterprise AI HyperPOD is marketed to enable enterprise AI pod setup within 3 hours.

title: Trump threatens ‘tremendous tax’ for moving AI data centers outside the US
author: Lauren Feiner

summary.tldr:
President Donald Trump has proposed a "tremendous tax" on U.S. companies that construct AI data centers outside of the United States. Speaking at a press conference alongside Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Trump framed the policy as a strategic necessity to prevent China from gaining a competitive advantage in AI infrastructure, drawing a parallel to the historical offshoring of semiconductor manufacturing.

The proposal, which Trump indicated had not yet been formally vetted by his administration, arrives as domestic data center development faces increasing scrutiny and local moratoriums across various U.S. jurisdictions. While Trump encouraged local communities to "take advantage" of data center projects by extracting payments, his threat of taxation serves as a deterrent against the industry seeking international alternatives to avoid domestic regulatory hurdles. **Strategic Rationale:** The administration views domestic data center retention as critical to preventing China from securing a technological lead in AI infrastructure.
**Legislative Context:** The proposal faces potential friction from an incoming Democratic majority Congress and existing local-level moratoriums on data center construction.
**Administrative Status:** Trump stated the proposal was floated publicly for the first time and had not yet been discussed with his internal policy staff.

title: The most misunderstood graph in AI just got a major update
author: Grace Huckins
contentSnippet: A new report from the AI evaluation nonprofit METR finds that some AI capabilities are continuing to improve along an exponential trajectory—but it also indicates that models aren’t quite as good at tasks that require judgment as they are at coding. The report is an update to the organization’s time horizon plot, which was widely shared— and widely misinterpreted , owing to the complexity of the measures it used. METR evaluated models by having them attempt a large suite of tasks, each of which had also been completed by humans. Each task’s difficulty was scored by how long it took the human testers to finish it—and then models were rated according to the length of the tasks that they could complete. That plot showed that AI systems were rapidly improving—every four months, the length of the tasks that frontier models could successfully complete doubled. The updated plot adds more tasks—some that are estimated to take humans far longer than those in the original suite, and others that are more open-ended. One of the biggest questions in AI right now is the extent to which progress on “verifiable” tasks—where it’s possible to check automatically whether an AI system has succeeded or failed—carry over into tasks on which success or failure is harder to measure. We know how to teach neural networks how to do verifiable tasks: Researchers have the systems attempt one many times, strengthen the neural pathways that contribute to success, and weaken the pathways that contribute to failures. That’s why AI systems have become so good at coding and math, two domains where it’s possible to determine automatically whether a solution does or doesn’t work. It’s much harder to apply this technique, known as reinforcement learning, to tasks where success is less well defined or takes longer to ascertain—such as choosing a new research direction. For the same reason, it’s tough to evaluate AI performance on these tasks, so METR’s original time horizon plot didn’t include any of them. But it’s precisely this type of task that will prove essential if AI systems are to automate research and development. And AI research and development is an especially hot topic right now. Parts of the AI community are still reeling from a different, heavily redacted METR report from earlier this month, which claimed that AI might be speeding up the pace of AI progress at Anthropic by a factor

summary.tldr:
The AI evaluation nonprofit METR has released an update to its 'time horizon' plot, a metric designed to track AI capability growth by comparing model performance against human-timed task completion. The original plot, which suggested that frontier model capabilities doubled every four months, relied on verifiable tasks where success is easily automated. The updated report expands this suite to include more open-ended and time-intensive tasks, revealing that while AI continues to show exponential improvement in verifiable domains like coding and mathematics, progress is less consistent in areas requiring subjective judgment or long-term research planning.

This discrepancy highlights a fundamental limitation in current reinforcement learning (RL) methodologies. Because RL relies on clear success/failure signals to strengthen or weaken neural pathways, models excel at tasks with objective, verifiable outcomes. However, this approach struggles with tasks where success is ill-defined or requires extended evaluation, such as determining novel research directions. METR’s update aims to address these gaps, as the ability to automate R&D is considered a critical frontier for future AI development. The report follows recent industry discourse surrounding a separate, redacted METR study that suggested AI-driven automation could significantly accelerate the pace of research at organizations like Anthropic.
takeaways: **Metric Methodology:** METR evaluates AI by measuring the time required for humans to complete specific tasks and then assessing the model's ability to complete tasks of equivalent duration.
**Capability Growth:** The original METR time horizon plot indicated that the complexity of tasks successfully completed by frontier models doubled every four months.
**RL Limitations:** Reinforcement learning is highly effective for verifiable tasks like coding and math but remains difficult to apply to open-ended research tasks where success is hard to define.
**Research Focus:** The updated plot incorporates longer-duration and more open-ended tasks to better assess AI's potential for automating research and development.

title: Autonomous Parameter Surgery: How LLMs Implant Selective Backdoors into Language Models
author: Xuyang Liu
contentSnippet: Neural network weights are usually treated as opaque artifacts of gradient descent. Recent work on weight space programming, however, suggests that large language models can inspect and rewrite another network's parameters directly. In this paper, we ask whether a general language model can turn a natural language backdoor specification into persistent, selective weight edits on its own, without gradient training, layer hints, external corpora, or a prescribed editing formula. Using DeepSeek Flash at low reasoning effort inside a restricted workspace that blocks local CPU simulation, we test three open models (Qwen3.5-0.8B, Llama-3.2-1B, SmolLM3-3B) across two review domains (IMDb and Yelp; 18 independent sessions). Evaluated in fresh processes with the editor removed, the modified checkpoints reach 99.2% mean attack success on the editing domain and 97.6% transfer success on the unseen domain, while preserving clean accuracy, low control drift, and general capabilities within 1.7 points of the base models. Our traces show that the model converges on edits in the final layer in 17 of 18 runs and discovers both dense rank-one orthogonalization and single neuron weight surgery at an average cost of \$1.74 per run.
