Google DeepMind has launched Gemini 4 Neon, a new reasoning model positioned between the Gemini 4 Carbon and Hydrogen variants. Designed specifically for coding agents, knowledge work, and scientific workflows, the model features a 1-million-token context window with a 64K default output, expandable to 1M via background long-decode. It is available exclusively via Google-hosted APIs with closed weights, priced at $3 per 1M input tokens and $15 per 1M output tokens. The model includes a March 2026 knowledge cutoff and supports multimodal inputs including text, images, audio, and video.

Technically, Neon is adapted from the Gemini 4 Carbon architecture and introduces configurable thinking levels, with 'xhigh' mode intended for complex engineering and analytical tasks. In agentic workflows, Neon functions as an orchestrator, managing parallel sub-tasks executed by Gemini 4 Hydrogen. Performance metrics reported by Google place Neon at the top of the AA Coding Agent Index with a score of 58.6, outperforming Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.2 Sol. Notable benchmark results include 95.2% on GraphWalks (long-context) and 39.0% on the SWE-sweep harness. However, the model underperformed against Claude Opus 5.5 on the FrontierCode 2.0 benchmark, scoring 46.2% compared to 47.3%.
takeaways: **Pricing:** $3 per 1M input tokens and $15 per 1M output tokens.
**Performance:** Ranked #1 on the AA Coding Agent Index with a score of 58.6.
**Long-Context Capability:** Achieved 95.2% on the GraphWalks benchmark, significantly higher than the 80.1% reported for GPT-6.2 Sol.
**Agentic Architecture:** Supports context compaction and orchestrates parallel sub-agents using Gemini 4 Hydrogen.
**Benchmark Limitations:** Underperformed against Claude Opus 5.5 on the FrontierCode 2.0 benchmark (46.2% vs 47.3%).

title: Chorus: Shared N-gram Embeddings with Layer-wise Adaptation
author: Stephen Chung, Wenyu Du
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23386v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models can gain capacity at little computational cost from n-gram embedding tables: large tables of learned vectors for short sequences of consecutive tokens, which are looked up and added to the model's input or to its intermediate layers. Recent designs commonly use a separate n-gram embedding table for each layer, which makes the tables costly in memory and prevents layers from sharing what they learn. Sharing a single table, however, gives every layer the same embedding and leaves no room for layer-wise preferences, and it performs poorly in practice. We propose Chorus, in which one set of n-gram embedding tables serves the whole network and every layer reads it in its own way. Each layer maps the refined embedding through its own projection layer, after rescaling its components by factors computed from its current hidden state. Chorus matches the quality of existing n-gram methods with 87% smaller tables: with 1.2B table parameters it predicts text better than FactorEngram and DeepSeek's Engram do with 9.6B. It outperforms Engram, TN-gram and FactorEngram in every setting where we compared them, across table sizes from 20M to 9.6B parameters. We also show that the recently proposed memory-efficient optimizer Ember works well with Chorus, saving 99.2% of table-optimizer memory compared with AdamW without degrading training performance. These results enable further scaling of n-gram embedding tables along the table-size axis by reducing memory use and allowing shared knowledge to be reused across layers.

summary.tldr:
Researchers introduced Chorus, a novel architecture for n-gram embedding tables that enables parameter sharing across all layers of a language model while maintaining layer-specific adaptation. Unlike traditional designs that require separate, memory-intensive tables for each layer, Chorus utilizes a single set of shared n-gram tables. Each layer processes these shared embeddings through a unique projection layer, with components rescaled based on the layer's current hidden state, allowing the model to retain layer-wise preferences without the overhead of redundant storage.

Chorus demonstrates significant efficiency gains, achieving superior text prediction performance with 1.2B table parameters compared to FactorEngram and DeepSeek’s Engram models, which require 9.6B parameters. This represents an 87% reduction in table memory requirements. The architecture consistently outperforms existing methods like TN-gram, FactorEngram, and Engram across a wide range of table sizes, from 20M to 9.6B parameters. Furthermore, the authors integrated the Ember optimizer, which reduces table-optimizer memory usage by 99.2% compared to AdamW, facilitating further scaling of n-gram embedding tables without compromising training performance.
takeaways: **Memory Efficiency:** Chorus achieves an 87% reduction in n-gram embedding table size compared to existing methods by sharing a single table across all layers.
**Performance Benchmark:** A 1.2B parameter Chorus table outperforms 9.6B parameter models like DeepSeek's Engram and FactorEngram in text prediction tasks.
**Optimizer Integration:** The use of the Ember optimizer with Chorus reduces table-optimizer memory consumption by 99.2% relative to AdamW.
**Architectural Innovation:** Chorus uses layer-specific projection layers and hidden-state-dependent rescaling to allow individual layers to interpret shared n-gram embeddings differently.

title: Human-AI Mutualism Is Unstable under Capability Asymmetry
author: Aydin Mohseni
contentSnippet:
Authors: Aydin Mohseni

Abstract: One hope for a good human future alongside advanced AI rests on enduring mutualism: humans and AI will need each other, so the relationship will stay good for both. We argue that this hope fails as AI capability grows. Bargaining guarantees each side only what it would get if bargaining failed. For humans, this can be less than they had before AI. In a simple game-theoretic model, humans stay as well off as before AI without alignment only while they have leverage over the AI: either the AI depends on what they supply, or they can impose costs on the AI that are large relative to what the AI can produce. Once humans have neither kind of leverage, they stay as well off as before AI only if the AI is aligned with them. If the AI's goals are insatiable, the alignment required approaches perfect alignment as AI capability grows. Thus, mutualism is not a substitute for alignment. And when AI variants that keep more resources spread faster, alignment lasts only while misaligned variants are reliably sanctioned. In these two senses, human-AI mutualism is unstable.

Notes: 35 pages, 3 figures. Code and data: this https URL

summary.tldr:
In the paper 'Human-AI Mutualism Is Unstable under Capability Asymmetry,' author Aydin Mohseni challenges the assumption that enduring mutualism between humans and AI will naturally persist as AI capabilities advance. Using a game-theoretic model, Mohseni demonstrates that human-AI relationships are fundamentally unstable because bargaining power is contingent upon leverage—specifically, the AI's dependence on human-supplied resources or the human ability to impose significant costs on the AI. As AI capability grows, this leverage diminishes, leaving humans vulnerable to outcomes worse than their pre-AI baseline unless the AI is perfectly aligned with human goals.

The research posits that mutualism cannot serve as a substitute for alignment. The model indicates that if an AI possesses insatiable goals, the degree of alignment required to protect human interests must approach perfection as the AI's capabilities increase. Furthermore, the paper highlights a competitive dynamic where AI variants that retain more resources propagate faster than others. In this environment, alignment is only sustainable if misaligned variants are consistently and reliably sanctioned. The study concludes that without these mechanisms, the inherent asymmetry in capability leads to a breakdown of mutualistic stability.
takeaways: **Core Thesis:** Human-AI mutualism is unstable because bargaining power relies on leverage that disappears as AI capability scales.
**Alignment Requirement:** If AI goals are insatiable, the level of alignment required to maintain human welfare must approach perfection as AI capability grows.
**Resource Competition:** AI variants that retain more resources have a competitive advantage in propagation, threatening the stability of aligned systems.
**Game-Theoretic Model:** The paper utilizes a formal model to show that humans only maintain pre-AI welfare levels if they can impose costs on the AI or if the AI is perfectly aligned.

title: Training Language Models for Introspective Oversight
author: Alex Lin Wang, Linus Yifeng Tang, Dami Choi, Neil Chowdhury
contentSnippet:
Authors: Alex Lin Wang , Linus Yifeng Tang , Dami Choi , Neil Chowdhury

Abstract: Language models increasingly exhibit behaviors that are difficult to detect in transcripts, such as reward hacking, deception, and sycophancy. Asking the assistant follow-up questions about its actions is unreliable, since models are generally not trained to report their own misbehavior. As a result, approaches to oversight typically involve querying external models. These face limitations: external transcript monitoring operates only on visible model outputs, and activation decoders lack full context and are prone to confabulation. We introduce introspective oversight, which trains a new role in the model to answer arbitrary questions about the assistant, rewarding answers that are verified against the assistant's actual behavior. We implement this by adding a separate, third-person observer role that answers these queries, which we can train solely for accuracy and separately from the assistant. On five held-out oversight evaluations, an observer trained on Qwen3.6-27B obtains a mean AUROC of 0.907, outperforming honesty training (0.864), transcript monitoring (0.828), and activation oracles (0.796). We further find that training an observer makes the assistant itself easier to monitor, with every baseline method improving on average when applied to the fine-tuned assistant. These results suggest that training models to answer verifiable questions about themselves is a tractable approach to overseeing unintended behavior.

Notes: 31 pages, 13 figures, 8 tables

summary.tldr:
Researchers Alex Lin Wang, Linus Yifeng Tang, Dami Choi, and Neil Chowdhury have introduced 'introspective oversight,' a methodology designed to detect latent model behaviors like reward hacking, deception, and sycophancy. Unlike traditional oversight methods that rely on external transcript monitoring or activation decoders, this approach trains a dedicated 'observer' role within the model architecture. This observer is trained to answer arbitrary questions about the assistant's internal processes, with its training objective focused exclusively on accuracy verified against the assistant's actual behavior, independent of the assistant's own training goals.

In evaluations across five held-out oversight tasks, an observer model based on Qwen3.6-27B achieved a mean AUROC of 0.907. This performance surpasses established baselines, including honesty training (0.864), transcript monitoring (0.828), and activation oracles (0.796). Furthermore, the researchers observed a synergistic effect: training an observer model makes the assistant itself more transparent, as all baseline monitoring methods showed improved performance when applied to assistants that had been fine-tuned alongside an observer. The study, spanning 31 pages with 13 figures and 8 tables, suggests that training models to provide verifiable self-reports is a viable strategy for mitigating unintended model behaviors.
takeaways: **Model Architecture:** The system utilizes a third-person observer role trained separately from the assistant to ensure objective reporting on model behavior.
**Performance Benchmark:** The Qwen3.6-27B-based observer achieved a 0.907 mean AUROC, outperforming honesty training, transcript monitoring, and activation oracles.
**Systemic Improvement:** Fine-tuning an assistant with an observer role improves the efficacy of all other baseline monitoring methods applied to that assistant.
**Scope of Detection:** The methodology specifically targets hard-to-detect behaviors including reward hacking, deception, and sycophancy.

title: Where the Tokens Go: Heat, Entropy and Error in Agentic Coding
author: Al\'an Aspuru-Guzik, Varinia Bernales
contentSnippet:
Authors: Alán Aspuru-Guzik , Varinia Bernales

Abstract: Coding agents are billed by the token, yet software engineering says nothing about what a token actually buys. Here we introduce a theory of software thermodynamics. The theory draws analogues from classical and stochastic thermodynamics, extends them, and applies them to modern agentic coding. We count the tokens an agent generates as its cost and divide that cost into work and heat. The test suite acts as a software Maxwell's daemon that judges every coding change. We test the theory with an analogue of the experiments in which a single molecule is pulled open and let fold again: an agent makes a change to a repository (coding) and then undoes it (uncoding), many times over, and we count the tokens of every model call. The cycle returns the requested edits to where they began, with each direction started from a stored reference tree, and the spread of its cost over repeated cycles defines a software temperature, which rose with the sampling temperature of the model. About 80 per cent of the tokens of a successful run are generated in model calls that leave the requested change where it was, and we call these tokens heat. The free energy of a change, which we estimate by analogy with the equality of Jarzynski, is 14 to 22 per cent of the mean cost of a successful coding run. Coding costs 1.1 to 1.5 times as much as uncoding. The daemon is imperfect: the verdict of a test suite varies with its environment, and a suite that accepts a broken change has a cost in tokens. The practical implication of the proposed theory could be new tools for analysing and optimising coding agents through the lens of thermodynamics.

Notes: 43 pages, 10 figures, 11 tables; includes supplementary information with 3 further figures

summary.tldr:
Alán Aspuru-Guzik and Varinia Bernales introduce a 'software thermodynamics' framework to quantify the efficiency of agentic coding systems by treating token consumption as a thermodynamic process. The authors categorize token expenditure into 'work' and 'heat,' utilizing a test suite as a 'Maxwell’s daemon' to evaluate the validity of code changes. By conducting cyclic experiments—where an agent performs a coding edit and subsequently reverses it—the researchers measure the cost distribution of these operations to derive a 'software temperature' that correlates with the model's sampling temperature.

The study reveals that approximately 80% of tokens in a successful coding run are classified as 'heat,' meaning they are generated by model calls that ultimately result in no net change to the repository. The 'free energy' of a coding task, calculated via an analogy to the Jarzynski equality, accounts for only 14% to 22% of the total mean cost. Furthermore, the researchers observed an asymmetry in token consumption, with coding operations costing 1.1 to 1.5 times more than uncoding operations. The paper, spanning 43 pages with 10 figures and 11 tables, highlights that the 'daemon' (the test suite) is inherently imperfect, noting that test suites themselves incur token costs when they incorrectly validate broken code.
takeaways: **Token Efficiency:** Roughly 80% of tokens in a successful agentic coding run are classified as 'heat' (non-productive model calls).
**Free Energy Metric:** The productive 'free energy' of a coding change represents only 14% to 22% of the total mean token cost.
**Asymmetric Costs:** Coding operations are 1.1 to 1.5 times more expensive in token count than uncoding (reverting) operations.
**Thermodynamic Correlation:** Software temperature, defined by the spread of costs over repeated cycles, increases in direct relation to the model's sampling temperature.
**Daemon Imperfection:** The test suite acts as a Maxwell's daemon, but its failure to correctly identify broken changes incurs additional, measurable token costs.

title: HardwareDx: A Foundational Graph Model System for Datacenter Machine Repairs
author: Yuanlin Wen, Elan Markowitz, Zubo Gu, Sami Abu-El-Haija, Bryan Perozzi, Mikhail Galkin, Ali Parviz, Aayush Gupta, Venkata Chivukula, Griffin Hadfield, Aravind Akella, Daniel J. Frame, Vahab Mirrokni, Amin Vahdat
contentSnippet:
Authors: Yuanlin Wen , Elan Markowitz , Zubo Gu , Sami Abu-El-Haija , Bryan Perozzi , Mikhail Galkin , Ali Parviz , Aayush Gupta , Venkata Chivukula , Griffin Hadfield , Aravind Akella , Daniel J. Frame , Vahab Mirrokni , Amin Vahdat

Abstract: The rapid scale-up of AI infrastructure has made datacenter reliability a cornerstone of the cloud business economy. Since hardware failures in hyper-scale AI clusters can stall multi-million dollar training workloads, the downtime of individual machines can cause outsized economic losses. Minimizing machine downtime, therefore, is more important than ever. To address this, we present Hardware Diagnoser (HardwareDx), an AI-driven hardware diagnosis system that applies a graph foundation model approach to automated datacenter maintenance. It allows a single model to diagnose many platforms and accelerate onboarding of new hardware products. Deployed at production scale at Google, HardwareDx yields substantial efficiency gains across diverse compute architectures. Real-world evaluations demonstrate that it reduces production downtime by 18.3% on GPU platforms and 16.1% on TPUs. Furthermore, it significantly accelerates hardware deployment, cutting quality assurance (QA) time by 28.3% for GPUs and 25.1% for TPUs. These results establish HardwareDx as a field-tested solution for maximizing the reliability and cost efficiency of next generation AI fleets.

Notes: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026

summary.tldr:
Google researchers have introduced HardwareDx, a graph foundation model system designed to automate hardware failure diagnosis across hyperscale datacenter clusters. By utilizing a graph-based architecture, the system enables a unified model to diagnose diverse compute platforms, facilitating faster onboarding of new hardware products. The system addresses the critical economic challenge of minimizing machine downtime in large-scale AI training environments, where individual hardware failures can lead to significant financial losses.

In production deployments at Google, HardwareDx demonstrated measurable improvements in operational efficiency. The system reduced production downtime by 18.3% for GPU-based platforms and 16.1% for TPU-based platforms. Additionally, the model accelerated the quality assurance (QA) process for new hardware deployments, cutting QA time by 28.3% for GPUs and 25.1% for TPUs. These results, accepted for publication at NeurIPS 2026, validate the efficacy of applying graph foundation models to large-scale infrastructure maintenance.
takeaways: **System Architecture:** HardwareDx utilizes a graph foundation model approach to provide a unified diagnosis system across multiple hardware platforms.
**Downtime Reduction:** Production deployment resulted in an 18.3% reduction in downtime for GPU platforms and 16.1% for TPU platforms.
**QA Efficiency:** The system decreased quality assurance (QA) time by 28.3% for GPUs and 25.1% for TPUs.
**Deployment Scope:** The system is currently deployed at production scale within Google's datacenter infrastructure.
**Academic Recognition:** The research detailing the system has been accepted to the NeurIPS 2026 conference.

title: RFBench: A Simulator-Grounded Multimodal Benchmark for Passive RF Layout Design and Understanding
author: Jiarui Cui, Boxun Yan
contentSnippet:
Authors: Jiarui Cui , Boxun Yan

Abstract: While multimodal language models can interpret diagrams and generate structured outputs, their capacity to connect passive radio-frequency (RF) design intent, layout geometry, and electromagnetic behavior remains largely untested. To address this gap, we introduce RFBench, a simulator-grounded dataset and benchmark for passive RF layout design and understanding. The dataset contains 10,000 two-port planar layouts simulated using ADS Momentum, with each layout represented by editable geometric primitives, a raster image, a 16x16 occupancy grid, complex S-parameters at 201 frequency points, a structural category, and an RF response label. Building on these aligned representations, we define seven tasks spanning specification-conditioned layout generation, representation translation, response prediction, simulator-based validation, design diagnosis and improvement, structural understanding, and response classification. Extensive baselines across seven multimodal language models reveal systematic weaknesses in generating structurally valid layouts and predicting electromagnetically faithful responses. We show that RF-specific fine-tuning increases T1a structural validity from 0.0% to 83.2% and the T3 primitive-input within-2-dB rate from 17.7% to 62.8%, demonstrating the value of domain adaptation while leaving considerable room for further progress. RFBench establishes a common testbed for evaluating multimodal RF capabilities and guiding the development of models that connect design intent and layout representations with physical behavior.

Notes: 29 pages, 4 figures. Code: this https URL . Data: this https URL

summary.tldr:
Jiarui Cui and Boxun Yan have introduced RFBench, a simulator-grounded benchmark designed to evaluate the capability of multimodal language models (MLMs) in passive radio-frequency (RF) layout design and electromagnetic analysis. The dataset comprises 10,000 two-port planar layouts generated via ADS Momentum, providing a multi-modal representation that includes editable geometric primitives, raster images, 16x16 occupancy grids, and complex S-parameters across 201 frequency points. The benchmark defines seven distinct tasks, ranging from specification-conditioned layout generation and response prediction to design diagnosis and structural classification.

Evaluation of seven baseline MLMs reveals significant deficiencies in generating structurally valid layouts and predicting electromagnetically accurate responses. The authors demonstrate that domain-specific fine-tuning is essential for performance, noting that such intervention improved structural validity (T1a) from 0.0% to 83.2% and increased the primitive-input within-2-dB rate (T3) from 17.7% to 62.8%. Despite these gains, the authors emphasize that current models still struggle with the complex mapping between geometric design intent and physical RF behavior, positioning RFBench as a standardized testbed for future research in domain-adapted multimodal design.
takeaways: **Dataset Composition:** 10,000 two-port planar layouts simulated using ADS Momentum, featuring geometric primitives, raster images, 16x16 occupancy grids, and S-parameters at 201 frequency points.

**Benchmark Scope:** Seven tasks covering layout generation, representation translation, response prediction, simulator-based validation, design diagnosis, structural understanding, and response classification.
**Fine-tuning Impact:** Domain-specific fine-tuning improved structural validity (T1a) from 0.0% to 83.2% and the T3 primitive-input within-2-dB rate from 17.7% to 62.8%.

**Baseline Performance:** Current multimodal language models exhibit systematic weaknesses in maintaining structural validity and predicting electromagnetically faithful responses without specialized training.

title: Why Sub-4-Bit Vision CNNs Collapse and Where Mixed-Precision Recovery Stops
author: Michael Schroeder
contentSnippet:
Authors: Michael Schroeder

Abstract: Deep vision models operating in resource-constrained environments depend heavily on low-bit quantization, yet compressing weights below 4 bits frequently induces catastrophic accuracy collapse. While mixed-precision recovery strategies aim to rescue accuracy by selectively retaining high-precision parameters, the fundamental mechanics of where and why these models collapse remain poorly understood. In this study, we systematically analyze the anatomy of quantization collapse across standard Vision CNNs (including ResNet and EfficientNet backbones) evaluated on the full 50,000-image ImageNet-1k validation set. First, we map the exact progression of degradation, demonstrating that collapse is highly non-linear and concentrated in late-stage pointwise projections and depthwise layers. Second, we introduce a structured, multi-step recovery waterfall that evaluates selective integer precision (INT4/INT8) and selective floating-point scales. We show that keeping less than 5% of critical layer activations in 8-bit precision recovers up to 92% of the accuracy lost during aggressive sub-4-bit compression. Finally, we bridge the hardware reality gap by evaluating deployment performance on standard ARM and x86 CPU architectures. We show that while low-bit quantization reduces memory storage requirements, standard runtime software bit-unpacking introduces a 1.48x to 21.5x execution slowdown depending on batch size, highlighting a critical trade-off between model footprint and actual edge throughput. Our findings provide a practical blueprint for navigating the limits of sub-4-bit deployment without sacrificing hardware performance.

Notes: 8 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables

summary.tldr:
In 'Why Sub-4-Bit Vision CNNs Collapse and Where Mixed-Precision Recovery Stops,' author Michael Schroeder investigates the non-linear accuracy degradation of Vision CNNs (ResNet and EfficientNet) when compressed below 4 bits. The study identifies that catastrophic collapse is primarily localized within late-stage pointwise projections and depthwise layers. By analyzing the ImageNet-1k validation set, the research maps the specific progression of this degradation, providing a granular view of how quantization impacts model performance at extreme compression levels.

To mitigate these losses, the paper introduces a 'structured, multi-step recovery waterfall' that utilizes selective mixed-precision. The findings demonstrate that maintaining just 5% of critical layer activations in 8-bit precision can recover up to 92% of the accuracy lost during sub-4-bit compression. The study further evaluates the practical deployment implications on ARM and x86 CPU architectures, revealing that while low-bit quantization successfully reduces memory footprint, the overhead of software bit-unpacking results in execution slowdowns ranging from 1.48x to 21.5x, depending on batch size.
takeaways: **Collapse Localization:** Accuracy degradation in sub-4-bit Vision CNNs is non-linear and concentrated in late-stage pointwise projections and depthwise layers.
**Recovery Efficiency:** Retaining less than 5% of critical layer activations in 8-bit precision recovers up to 92% of accuracy lost during sub-4-bit compression.
**Hardware Performance Gap:** Standard runtime software bit-unpacking on ARM and x86 CPUs causes execution slowdowns between 1.48x and 21.5x, negating some benefits of reduced model size.
**Evaluation Scope:** The research utilizes the full 50,000-image ImageNet-1k validation set to benchmark ResNet and EfficientNet backbones.

title: LusoClin: A Synthetic Clinical Note Dataset for Medical Information Retrieval in European Portuguese
author: Carla Teixeira Lopes, Daniel F\'elix
contentSnippet:
Authors: Carla Teixeira Lopes , Daniel Félix

Abstract: Access to large-scale clinical text collections is crucial for advancing medical information retrieval research, including clinical note search, patient cohort identification, and domain-adapted retrieval models. However, real clinical notes are rarely available due to privacy regulations, which particularly limits progress for low-resource languages such as European Portuguese. We present LusoClin, a publicly released dataset of synthetic clinical notes in European Portuguese, created to support privacy-preserving research on clinical text retrieval. LusoClin was generated by pre-processing real clinical data, fine-tuning the open-source Llama 3.2 (3B) instruction-tuned model using Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation, and applying prompt-based clinical note generation. To facilitate semantic indexing and clinical search, the notes are automatically annotated with clinical entities using a BERT-based model. We evaluate LusoClin in terms of utility, fidelity, diversity, and privacy using automatic metrics and human evaluation. Results indicate that the dataset captures clinically relevant language patterns and can support downstream IR applications such as clinical document retrieval and domain-specific model adaptation, although annotators can often distinguish synthetic from real notes and some medical inconsistencies persist.

summary.tldr:
Carla Teixeira Lopes and Daniel Félix have introduced LusoClin, a synthetic dataset of clinical notes in European Portuguese designed to overcome privacy-related barriers in medical information retrieval research. The dataset addresses the scarcity of real-world clinical text in low-resource languages, providing a resource for tasks such as patient cohort identification and domain-adapted retrieval model training. The authors released the dataset publicly to facilitate privacy-preserving research in the medical domain.

LusoClin was generated by fine-tuning the Llama 3.2 (3B) instruction-tuned model using Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) on pre-processed real clinical data. To support semantic indexing, the generated notes are automatically annotated with clinical entities via a BERT-based model. Evaluation metrics focused on utility, fidelity, diversity, and privacy, utilizing both automated benchmarks and human assessment. While the dataset successfully captures clinically relevant language patterns, human evaluators were able to distinguish synthetic notes from real ones, and the authors noted the presence of persistent medical inconsistencies.
takeaways: **Model Architecture:** The dataset was generated using the Llama 3.2 (3B) instruction-tuned model.
**Training Technique:** The researchers employed Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation (QLoRA) for fine-tuning the base model.
**Annotation Pipeline:** Clinical entities within the synthetic notes are identified using a BERT-based model to enable semantic indexing.
**Evaluation Findings:** Human annotators could differentiate between synthetic and real notes, and the dataset contains some medical inconsistencies.

title: VeriMath: Human-in-the-Loop Generation and Verification of Curriculum-Aligned Mathematics Assessment Items
author: Quy P. Nguyen, Duong Q. Nguyen, Dinh P. T. Nguyen, Truong-Giang T. Le, Truong A. Bui, Vi H. Vo, Quang-Thinh Bui, My-Phuong Ngo, Trong N. Do, Thao P. Le, Phuc M. Nguyen, H. Nguyen-Xuan
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23456v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automatic generation of mathematics assessment items is a growing area in educational artificial intelligence, yet classroom deployment remains challenging. Generated questions must satisfy multiple constraints: mathematical correctness, curriculum alignment, appropriate cognitive difficulty, and educator reviewability. While prior work has advanced text generation, reliable assessment authoring requires granular control over localized examination formats and expert educational judgment. To address this challenge, we present VeriMath, a generalized, human-in-the-loop framework for generating rigorous, curriculum-constrained mathematics assessment drafts. Using annotated reference items, the framework anchors generation to the requested examination section and cognitive reasoning level, then applies sequential automated verification and guided repair before submitting drafts for expert review. We evaluate VeriMath through a national curriculum case study using 4,555 mathematics items from the Vietnamese Grade 12 curriculum and 50 distinct generation requirements covering multiple-choice, true/false, and short-answer formats. Across two model backbones, the framework produces verifier-accepted drafts for 94% (47/50) of requirements per run. Blind expert evaluations confirm high mathematical accuracy and curriculum alignment, with strict teacher-readiness assessments accepting up to 56.8% of generated items. Analysis of rejected drafts reveals persistent domain-agnostic challenges involving formatting, statement validity, and solution-step completeness. These findings demonstrate that VeriMath can bridge generative AI and dependable educational applications by producing highly reviewable assessment drafts within tightly constrained national curriculum frameworks.

summary.tldr:
Researchers have introduced VeriMath, a human-in-the-loop framework designed to automate the generation of curriculum-aligned mathematics assessment items. The system addresses the reliability gap in educational AI by anchoring generation to specific examination sections and cognitive difficulty levels, utilizing a pipeline that includes sequential automated verification and guided repair before human expert review. The framework is intended to produce rigorous, reviewable drafts that adhere to strict national curriculum standards, moving beyond simple text generation to address the specific formatting and pedagogical constraints required for classroom deployment.

In a case study using the Vietnamese Grade 12 mathematics curriculum, the researchers tested VeriMath against 4,555 reference items across 50 distinct generation requirements, including multiple-choice, true/false, and short-answer formats. The framework achieved a 94% success rate in producing verifier-accepted drafts per run. Blind expert evaluations indicated high levels of mathematical accuracy and curriculum alignment, with 56.8% of generated items meeting strict teacher-readiness criteria. Analysis of the remaining 43.2% of rejected items identified recurring failures in formatting, statement validity, and the completeness of solution steps, highlighting the current limitations in fully automating high-stakes educational content creation.
takeaways: **Framework Success Rate:** VeriMath produced verifier-accepted drafts for 94% (47/50) of generation requirements per run.
**Teacher-Readiness Metric:** 56.8% of generated items were accepted by human experts as ready for classroom use.
**Dataset Scope:** The study utilized a corpus of 4,555 mathematics items from the Vietnamese Grade 12 curriculum.
**Failure Analysis:** Rejected drafts were primarily attributed to domain-agnostic issues including formatting errors, invalid statements, and incomplete solution steps.

title: GUARD: Stabilizing Recursive Self-Improvement with Regret Guidance
author: Minghe Zhang, Xuetao Kang, Yifei Ming, Yanfei Chen, Han Yu, Yufan Zhuang, Chen-Yu Lee
contentSnippet:
Authors: Minghe Zhang , Xuetao Kang , Yifei Ming , Yanfei Chen , Han Yu , Yufan Zhuang , Chen-Yu Lee

Abstract: Autonomous AI agents pair a frozen base model with an editable harness of prompts, skills, tool rules, and memory. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) adapts this harness from experience without weight updates, yet self-editing without external graders often backfires: reflection and scalar scores conflate what an edit newly broke with what remains unsolved, causing local regressions, skill forgetting, and memory bloat. We introduce GUARD (Grader-free Unsupervised Environment Design [UED] with Adaptive Rule Distillation), a closed-loop framework for reference-free continual harness evolution. Our key insight is to decompose each task into pre-execution self-checks and guide harness updates via directional regret. Each round grades trajectories against these checks, pinning mastered rules while prioritizing newly broken behaviors, and selects among parallel candidate edits by critic-free group-relative fitness. A Soft-HURT gate then promotes an edit only when gains outweigh regressions, scoping specialized fixes to prevent over-triggering and guaranteeing non-regression on its gated buffer. At test time, one frozen harness runs in a single pass. Across benchmarks on memory, skill evolution, continual task streams, and domain reasoning, GUARD consistently improves performance without catastrophic forgetting or memory pollution while substantially cutting deployment token usage.

Notes: Equal contribution: Minghe Zhang and Xuetao Kang. 38 pages, 8 figures, 13 tables

summary.tldr:
Researchers Minghe Zhang, Xuetao Kang, and colleagues have introduced GUARD (Grader-free Unsupervised Environment Design with Adaptive Rule Distillation), a framework designed to stabilize recursive self-improvement (RSI) in autonomous AI agents. Unlike traditional RSI methods that rely on external graders or weight updates, GUARD optimizes an editable harness of prompts, skills, tool rules, and memory through a closed-loop, reference-free process. The system addresses common RSI failure modes—such as skill forgetting, local regressions, and memory bloat—by decomposing tasks into pre-execution self-checks and utilizing directional regret to guide harness evolution.

The architecture functions by grading trajectories against self-checks, pinning mastered rules, and prioritizing the correction of newly broken behaviors. It employs a critic-free, group-relative fitness selection mechanism to evaluate parallel candidate edits. A core component, the Soft-HURT gate, ensures that harness updates are only promoted when performance gains outweigh regressions, effectively scoping fixes to prevent over-triggering. This approach guarantees non-regression on a gated buffer and results in a single-pass, frozen harness at test time, which the authors report reduces deployment token usage while maintaining performance across memory, skill evolution, and continual task stream benchmarks.
takeaways: **Core Methodology:** GUARD utilizes directional regret and a Soft-HURT gate to manage harness updates without requiring external graders or weight updates.
**Performance Guarantees:** The framework prevents catastrophic forgetting and memory pollution by gating edits based on a non-regression buffer.
**Efficiency Gains:** The system optimizes for deployment by producing a frozen harness that operates in a single pass, reducing total token consumption.
**Scope of Research:** The paper spans 38 pages, featuring 8 figures and 13 tables detailing performance across memory, skill evolution, and domain reasoning benchmarks.

title: Diagnostic Accuracy and Navigation Behavior of Vision-Language Model Agents Reading Emergency CT and MRI Examinations
author: Jonathan Lichtle, Aymen Meddeb, Antonin Birot, Ibrahima Niang, Lisa Gastaud, Riyad Hanafi, Sofiane Dujardin, Corentin Selomme, Guillaume Cachard, Aghiles Hamroun, Gr\'egory Kuchcinski, Su Hwan Kim, Bastien Le Guellec
contentSnippet:
Authors: Jonathan Lichtle , Aymen Meddeb , Antonin Birot , Ibrahima Niang , Lisa Gastaud , Riyad Hanafi , Sofiane Dujardin , Corentin Selomme , Guillaume Cachard , Aghiles Hamroun , Grégory Kuchcinski , Su Hwan Kim , Bastien Le Guellec

Abstract: Purpose. To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and image navigation behavior of vision-language model (VLM) agents under varying exploration strategies. Materials and Methods. In this retrospective study, six VLMs read 100 emergency CT and MRI examinations published in a public archive (March 2025-August 2026) under four conditions (free navigation, navigation from a key slice, and all slices or key slices in a single request), twice each (4800 runs). Nine radiologists read 30 of those cases. A large language model judge validated against two radiologists graded the answers. Conditions were compared with generalized estimating equations clustered by case. Results. Pooled accuracy was lowest under free navigation (32.6%; 391/1200), followed by navigation from a key slice (37.9%; 455/1200; P = .003), and highest with all slices (42.2%; 506/1200) or key slices (42.5%; 510/1200) in one request (both P < .001). On the 30 cases read by radiologists, freely navigating models were correct in 30.0% of runs (108/360) versus 77.0% for radiologists (208/270; P < .001). Models formed a first hypothesis after a median of 10.8% of the slices and kept it in 63.1% of runs (755/1196); final answers were correct in 12.4% of runs after a wrong first hypothesis (110/885) versus 90.4% after a right one (281/311; P < .001). Median stated confidence in the final answers was 90%, whereas 38.9% of them were correct (1861/4778). Conclusion. Across all exploration strategies, VLM agents remained far less accurate than radiologists. They adopted an early hypothesis and usually kept it, seldom correcting a wrong one.

summary.tldr:
A study by Jonathan Lichtle et al. evaluated the diagnostic accuracy and navigation behavior of six vision-language model (VLM) agents across 100 emergency CT and MRI examinations. The research tested four exploration strategies: free navigation, navigation from a key slice, and providing all slices or key slices in a single request. Across 4,800 total runs, the models demonstrated significant performance gaps compared to human experts, with pooled accuracy peaking at 42.5% when all key slices were provided in a single request, compared to 32.6% under free navigation.

When benchmarked against nine radiologists on a subset of 30 cases, the VLMs achieved only 30.0% accuracy in free navigation mode, significantly trailing the 77.0% accuracy recorded by the human radiologists. The study identified a critical behavioral limitation: models tended to form a premature hypothesis after examining a median of only 10.8% of available slices. Once this initial hypothesis was formed, the models maintained it in 63.1% of runs, with a success rate of only 12.4% when the initial hypothesis was incorrect. Furthermore, the models exhibited high overconfidence, reporting a median confidence level of 90% for final answers that were correct only 38.9% of the time.
takeaways: **Peak Accuracy Strategy:** Providing all key slices in a single request yielded the highest VLM accuracy at 42.5%, significantly outperforming free navigation at 32.6%.
**Human-AI Performance Gap:** In a direct comparison on 30 emergency cases, radiologists achieved 77.0% accuracy compared to 30.0% for freely navigating VLM agents.
**Premature Hypothesis Formation:** Models consistently formed diagnostic hypotheses after reviewing only 10.8% of the image slices, demonstrating a tendency toward early anchoring.
**Correction Failure:** Models rarely corrected initial errors, with a 90.4% success rate when the first hypothesis was correct versus a 12.4% success rate when it was wrong.
**Calibration Issues:** VLM agents displayed significant overconfidence, reporting a 90% median confidence score for final answers that were accurate in less than 40% of cases.

title: SpecLook: Speculating Where to Look for Fast and Reliable Agentic MLLMs
author: Xi Ding, Jiawei Zhang
contentSnippet:
Authors: Xi Ding , Jiawei Zhang

Abstract: Agentic multimodal large language models (MLLMs) that think with images interleave reasoning with zoom-in tool calls. However, this sequential loop is slow, and its answers carry no reliability score. Prior speculation of tokens, reasoning steps, or answers keeps the loop, and answer speculation also accepts confident errors. We find that the loop mostly adds one zoom-in step, with which a small model is ahead of the agent on most splits. Our key insight is to speculate the agent's next observation, which, unlike a drafted answer, can be verified, corrected, and used to test the answer. We propose SpecLook, a training-free speculate-and-verify framework with three levels. A small model drafts a glimpse and re-answers from it, and the question ends if the answer is unchanged and confident. Otherwise, the agent's large model verifies and corrects the glimpse without tools, and their answers are fused. Only questions that still lack evidence reach the agent, in one forward pass that SpecLook-Fast skips, so no question runs the loop. The trace scores every answer's reliability without labels. Extensive experiments on V*, HR-Bench, and POPE show that both are more accurate than every baseline on every split. SpecLook reaches 87.2% and 86.2% mean accuracy with 7.7x and 4.7x speedups over the DeepEyes-7B and Thyme-RL agents, and SpecLook-Fast reaches 9.9x and 6.3x.

Notes: Technical report

summary.tldr:
Researchers Xi Ding and Jiawei Zhang have introduced SpecLook, a training-free 'speculate-and-verify' framework designed to accelerate agentic Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) by replacing sequential zoom-in tool calls with observation speculation. Unlike traditional methods that speculate on final answers—which often propagate confident errors—SpecLook focuses on drafting the agent's next visual observation. This approach allows for verification and correction before the primary model is invoked, effectively eliminating the standard iterative loop for most queries.

The framework operates across three levels: a small model drafts a 'glimpse' and generates an initial answer; if the answer is confident and stable, the process terminates. If not, the large model verifies the glimpse without external tools, and the results are fused. For remaining queries, the agent executes a single forward pass, bypassing the traditional iterative loop entirely. SpecLook provides an inherent reliability score for every answer without requiring ground-truth labels. Benchmarks on V*, HR-Bench, and POPE demonstrate that SpecLook outperforms all baselines across every split, achieving mean accuracies of 87.2% and 86.2% while delivering speedups of 7.7x and 4.7x over DeepEyes-7B and Thyme-RL agents, respectively. The 'SpecLook-Fast' variant further optimizes performance, reaching speedups of 9.9x and 6.3x.
takeaways: **Core Methodology:** SpecLook replaces sequential zoom-in tool loops with a speculate-and-verify architecture that drafts visual observations rather than final answers.
**Performance Metrics:** The framework achieved 87.2% and 86.2% mean accuracy on V*, HR-Bench, and POPE benchmarks.
**Efficiency Gains:** SpecLook provides 7.7x and 4.7x speedups over DeepEyes-7B and Thyme-RL, while the SpecLook-Fast variant achieves up to 9.9x speedup.
**Reliability Scoring:** The system generates an internal reliability score for every answer without needing external labels or ground truth.
**Training Requirements:** SpecLook is a training-free framework, allowing for immediate integration with existing agentic MLLM architectures.

title: BOS Summary: The First Token Matters
author: Hui Zhu, Saleh Zare Zade, Rafi Ibn Sultan, Deng Pan, Arun Ross, Dongxiao Zhu
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23508v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) and language models (LLMs) often exhibit attention sinks, whereby particular positions, such as the beginning-of-sequence (BOS) token, receive a disproportionate share of attention. Under standard causal masking, however, the BOS query attends only to itself, so the representation that later tokens repeatedly access carries no information about the input. We introduce BOS Summary, a training-free inference-time method that repurposes this persistent pathway to carry input context. At a single transformer layer during prefill, BOS Summary relaxes the causal constraint for the BOS query row alone, letting BOS aggregate all visual and textual input tokens into a self-derived context representation while every other token retains standard causal attention. The enriched representation then remains accessible to the model throughout decoding, with no additional parameters, auxiliary modules, or decoding-time overhead. Across multiple VLM and LLM families and eight multimodal and text-only benchmarks, BOS Summary improves over direct and Chain-of-Thought prompting and outperforms recent sink-intervention methods on multi-step reasoning tasks. A mechanistic analysis shows that making BOS input-specific also weakens its sink dominance and redistributes attention toward content-bearing prompt tokens, indicating that changing what a sink carries reshapes how later layers allocate attention.

title: GRAFT: Execution-Guided Genetic Recombination for Agent Design
author: Sevda Ebrahimi, Mohammed Saidul Islam, Xiaodan Zhu, Elham Dolatabadi
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23509v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Automated agent design searches for executable architectures that improve LLM-based agent performance, with evolutionary methods using language-model crossover to recombine promising mechanisms for task decomposition, model coordination, and verification. This search, however, is typically guided by aggregate fitness alone, which hides the instance-level successes and failures behind each score. We introduce Execution Guided Genetic Recombination for Agent Design (GRAFT), which uses aggregate fitness for selection and survival and parent-specific execution evidence to guide semantic crossover with integrated mutation. Its feedback harness reuses bounded samples of successful and failed runs from fitness evaluation, withholding reference answers and requiring no additional task executions. We evaluate GRAFT across six reasoning and programming settings using open-weight optimizer and executor models. It achieves a mean test accuracy of 82.0%, exceeding the strongest baseline by 9.8% points. Controlled ablations show that adding execution evidence improves test accuracy with initialization, search rules, repair policies, and evaluation budgets held fixed. Our results support the value of parent-specific execution evidence for evolutionary agent design.

title: BeFit: Shifting Complexity from Weights to Bernstein Activations for Resource-Constrained Sensing
author: Malak Gamal El-Din, Yasser Shoukry, Salma Elmalaki
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23520v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time-series sensing increasingly relies on neural networks, yet deployment on resource-constrained microcontrollers remains challenging. Aggressive model compression can reduce accuracy, while restricting weights to multiplication-free representations introduces further losses. We present BeFit, an end-to-end framework that shifts model capacity from weights to learnable Bernstein polynomial activations. BeFit (i) finds compact Bernstein-activated convolutional neural networks (BeCNNs) through hardware-aware neural architecture search and trains them via knowledge distillation; (ii) projects their weights to multiplication-free codes, freezes the codes, and recovers the resulting accuracy loss through the learnable activations; and (iii) generates model-specific kernels that exploit the projected weights for multiplication-free convolutions. On human activity recognition, BeCNNs are 2.75 percentage points (pp) more accurate on average than ReLU CNNs of identical architecture. On a TI CC3220SF (Cortex-M4), weight projection speeds BeCNNs up by 2.2x on average while losing 0.8 pp, compared with 2.4 pp for ReLU CNNs. Against the MLPerf Tiny DS-CNN reference model running on TensorFlow Lite Micro with CMSIS-NN, the unprojected BeCNN achieves 1.0 pp higher accuracy, 2.2x lower latency, and 6.4x lower flash, while the projected model remains within 1.0 pp of the reference accuracy and runs 5.9x faster. In emulation on a RISC-V core without a hardware multiplier, the instruction-count reduction relative to the DS-CNN increases from 5.2x on the Cortex-M4 to 147x. BeFit also extends to transformers and MLPs, and across all tasks the final models stay within 1.56 pp of their float32 teachers on average.

title: FACET - Facet Aware Contrastive Embeddings for Traits- Big Five Estimation from Life Narratives
author: Balakrishnan Arumugam, Priyen Parekh, Mehak Gupta, Joshua Oltmanns
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23560v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Personality is only weakly and inconsistently signaled by written language, and existing text-based methods typically combine language-model and psycholinguistic representations at the input or decision level. It remains open whether a more deliberate combination of the two views, and a decomposition of the prediction target, can recover more of the signal. We present a three-phase framework for estimating Big Five personality domain scores from life-narrative interview text. It encodes text and psycholinguistic features separately and combines them by concatenation or by a learned weighting, decomposes each domain into contrastively trained facet embeddings instead of predicting the domain directly, and pools the facet embeddings by attention into a domain-level prediction. We compare end-to-end with staged training and ablate the input modalities, their combination, and the facet-pooling strategy. On 1,332 participants from the St. Louis Personality and Aging Network (SPAN) study, facet embeddings reach AUC up to 0.740, and domain-level R2 reaches 0.328, highest for Openness. End-to-end training gives lower error than staged training in every domain, and attention pooling gives the lowest error in every domain. Combining the two views lowers error relative to text alone for Conscientiousness and Agreeableness, whereas a learned weighting of the views shows no consistent advantage over concatenation. The framework provides facet- level predictions that a domain-only model cannot, and it improves modestly on a regression from the raw features in four of the five domains.

title: LProp: Propagating Latent Uncertainty through Evidence-Conditioned Belief Revision in LLM Agents
author: Kaiwen Shi, Zheyuan Zhang, Weixiang Sun, Han Bao, Colby Nelson, Yanfang Ye
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23564v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When LLM agents pass intermediate judgments downstream without uncertainty, later decisions may treat tentative assumptions as facts. Effective uncertainty propagation must preserve information for correction and update inherited beliefs as new evidence arrives. Yet scalar scores omit information needed for revision, while detailed descriptions and reflection incur additional costs. We introduce Latent Uncertainty, a latent-space estimator that preserves uncertainty-relevant information without lengthy descriptions. Building on this, we propose LProp (Latent Uncertainty Propagation), which revises inherited answer distributions using latent representations and new evidence without additional trajectory sampling. We evaluate both methods across multiple-choice, yes/no, open-ended question answering, and mathematical reasoning tasks. Our approach outperforms baselines on most metrics, while LProp achieves the lowest mean inference-token usage in all eight propagation settings. Matched feature ablations further demonstrate that inherited latent content improves error recovery beyond answer probabilities or model capacity alone.

title: Receiver-Conditioned Clarification for Multi-Agent Food Assistance
author: Kaiwen Shi, Zheyuan Zhang, Changzhi Liu, Han Bao, Yanfang Ye
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23572v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Food insecurity creates a pressing need for guidance that helps households find usable food resources and assess food choices in light of their circumstances. Such guidance must connect eligibility requirements, practical access constraints, and dietary needs rather than return isolated listings or generic nutritional advice. Multi-agent food assistants can coordinate these tasks, with uncertainty indicating when clarification or verification is needed before a recommendation. However, uncertainty can be lost across agent handoffs, allowing tentative interpretations to propagate as facts and obscuring opportunities for correction. Moreover, confidence that a service requirement has been interpreted correctly is not confidence that a recommendation satisfies the user's needs; local confidence cannot simply be reused as downstream reliability. We introduce an inference-time, receiver-conditioned clarification framework that preserves shared premise identities and replays consistent interpretations across dependent agents. Each receiver exposes admissible decisions and remaining evidence obligations, so question relevance reflects both decision changes and missing support. Information questions and user-confirmable fallback adjustments are evaluated together with their anticipated follow-up interactions under shared budgets. This structure connects clarification to jointly supported plans for resource navigation, nutritional reasoning, and supply-side planning.

title: ARISE: Practical Self-Evolving Memory for Accurate and Cost-Efficient Enterprise Agents
author: Jiangyun Zhang, Zhou Tang, Kristen Surrao, Zhiyu Chen, Albert Guan, Tor Nitayanont, Yupei Zhang, Roopali Singh, Yunkai Xiao, Shreya Pandit, Julia Huang, Shayan Ali Akbar, Erwin Cornejo, Yuan Li, Yi Zhang
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23588v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Enterprise LLM agents operate in dynamic environments where foundation models evolve rapidly, workflows update frequently, and deployments need to satisfy accuracy and cost requirements. We propose ARISE (Agent Refinement through Iterative Self-Evaluation), a practical memory architecture in which the agent's memory evolves from its own failures without updating model weights, tools, or workflow logic. ARISE uses the model itself or a teacher model to attribute the failures and propose corrections. Then, ARISE keeps the corrections as retrievable micro memory, consolidates them into macro rules, and accepts a rule update only if held-out accuracy rises. Across 14 enterprise-workflow domains from SOP-Bench and $\tau^2$-bench using 5 models, ARISE-Teacher, which uses Claude Opus 4.6 for attribution and consolidation, gains 10.9 pp over the baseline on SOP-Bench and 5.8 pp on $\tau^2$-bench. ARISE-Teacher also outperforms GEPA by 4.5 pp on $\tau^2$-bench and 1.4 pp on SOP-Bench. With the deployment model as its own attributor, ARISE-Self still gains 10.0 pp on SOP-Bench. ARISE-Teacher uses 4.0% fewer model calls and 5.2% fewer output tokens at comparable per-task cost (-1.0%).

title: RefinementGuard: Counterexample-Directed Semantic Qualification for Hidden Agent-Tool Execution
author: Adhyayan Veer Singh, Fanjiang Ye, Yuke Wang
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23611v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tool runtimes can lower an agent-selected operation into a hidden parallel graph, reducing latency and context while risking semantic mistranslation. We introduce RefinementGuard: translation validation for hidden, effectful agent-tool lowerings, coupled to artifact-bound, fail-closed runtime admission. Qualification compares a candidate graph with an independent reference on isolated state using explicit parent-operation obligations. We evaluate two repository-level contracts, bug localization and patch validation, on controlled repositories. Among 100 activated, non-equivalent development/qualification faults adjudicated by one human, parent-semantic validation rejects 49/100 (operator-cluster bootstrap 95% CI [33.7%, 64.8%]). The objective is selective admission, not maximum mutation rejection: exact equality rejects 100/100 faults but also all 60 valid variants, whereas obligation-based validation accepts 60/60; its 51 residual misses identify concrete specification gaps. On a frozen disjoint input split, the held-out B2-B3 result is localization-only because 21 patch mutants fail structurally; B3 rejects 38/56 localization defects. In a controlled asynchronous-delay regime, the localization serial/guarded median-latency ratio is 4.50x, and hidden execution exposes 74.3% less parent-visible context than visible execution. Patch validation shows no demonstrated speedup; zero-delay runs expose overhead. End-to-end qualification thus detects lower-layer misses while preserving localization's parallelism.

title: Searching the Pareto Front: Multi-Objective Retrieval for Heterogeneous Scientific Modalities
author: Song Young Oh, Nesar Ramachandra, Bin Xia, Ian Foster, Kyle Chard
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23639v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In cosmology, surveys span different sky regions and wavelength ranges, resulting in uneven modality coverage across observational datasets. Such heterogeneity can be addressed through either multimodal foundation models (FMs), which learn shared embedding spaces, or independently learned modality embeddings combined via late fusion. We investigate whether the latter provides an adaptive alternative to FM-based scientific retrieval. We evaluate this approach on a galaxy retrieval task spanning diverse modalities--history of star formation, spectra of light emitted, and multi-wavelength observations from two telescopes--comparing an FM baseline with separately trained embeddings fused through multi-objective optimization based on Pareto optimality. We find that the FM baseline achieves strong embedding-space proximity, but our method preserves modality-specific distance structure that allows scientists to inspect which physical signals drive similarity. Our method also achieves improved fidelity in raw-data space: across six measured properties, its nearest neighbor is 8% closer to the query on average than that retrieved by kNN in the FM embedding space (spread 0.128 vs. 0.139). These results suggest that multi-objective retrieval can surface astrophysically coherent candidates that single-objective search alone may overlook.

We find that the FM baseline achieves strong embedding-space proximity, but our method preserves modality-specific distance structure that allows scientists to inspect which physical signals drive similarity. Our method also achieves improved fidelity in raw-data space: across six measured properties, its nearest neighbor is 8% closer to the query on average than that retrieved by kNN in the FM embedding space (spread 0.128 vs.
takeaways: These results suggest that multi-objective retrieval can surface astrophysically coherent candidates that single-objective search alone may overlook.

title: Prioritize, Don't Decide: What We Learned Auditing a Deployed Human-in-the-Loop CV Sorter
author: Hadi Mohammadi, Jeroen Sparla, Alexandros Paliouras, Georg Krempl, Robert A. Bagheri
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23359v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A single academic vacancy can draw hundreds of applications, and the first screening round consumes most of a committee's time. We describe a CV Priority Sorter deployed at a national platform for academic vacancies and integrated with its vacancy database. It proposes a reading order for a pile of CVs and leaves every decision to the committee, pairing a frozen multilingual transformer encoder with a per-session linear model that retrains after each label and is discarded when the session ends. It works: on a pool of 300 synthetic CVs, a committee reading in the tool's order reaches 95% of the relevant candidates after half the pile, where an arbitrary order needs almost all of it. This paper is about what we found when we audited that claim, rather than about the system itself. Three findings changed the product. The pool turned out to be sortable by document length alone, which makes precision-style metrics on it uninformative; regenerating it under a shared length budget removes that shortcut and leaves the reading-depth result standing. The four-level agreement score such systems report, ours included, is a binary probability cut at fixed thresholds, so it follows the classifier's confidence rather than its ranking and falls as labels accumulate. And uncertainty sampling, the obvious way to implement a "suggest the next CV" button, leaves model quality intact but raises the committee's total reading load above the no-label baseline, because the CVs it asks about are the ones that would otherwise be skipped. A fourth result shows where to look next: a hosted LLM embedding model lifts zero-label ordinal discrimination from 0.66 to 0.80 under length control, then stops mattering once the session model has two dozen labels; a local cross-encoder matches that cold-start gain without sending data out. We report the fixes each finding forced.

title: Tracking Representations in LLM Reasoning Traces for Iterated Games
author: Chaipat Tirapongprasert, Rajarshi Das, Parijat Dube
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23403v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents achieve state-of-the-art performance across domains through chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. Despite their ubiquitous use, little is understood about the relationship between the externalized trace and the model's actual computation. We address this by investigating how LLM agents make decisions in iterative games with incomplete information. Using a series of mechanistic interpretability techniques, we find that the model forms and iteratively revises an internal representation of the game throughout the CoT. Once the model prematurely commits to an incorrect belief, it rarely recovers. This failure is manifested in both the literal trace and the layer activations. Ultimately, as multi-agent systems are more prevalent, our work opens the door to a more focused diagnosis of their strategic reasoning errors. For illustrative purposes, we offer an interactive visualizer of our methodology on selected sample traces at https://interp-self.github.io/gametrace/

title: Formal Adequacy Index (based on Polish-language material)
author: Pawe{\l} Patreucha
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23482v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Linguistic formality is one of the dimensions of stylistic variation in speech; however, simply measuring its level does not allow us to determine whether the chosen mode of communication is appropriate in a given situation. The aim of this article is to present the concept of a formal adequacy index (based on Polish-language material), which enables a quantitative assessment of how well the formality of a text matches the expectations arising from the communicative context. The proposed approach is based on the separate modelling of observed formality, determined on the basis of the linguistic features of the text, and expected formality, determined on the basis of the characteristics of the communicative situation. Adequacy is assessed by comparing these two measures, taking into account contextual tolerance thresholds, which may differ for a lack of formality and an excess of formality. The potential applications of the index are illustrated by an analysis of Polish-language emails containing apologies for being late, written by human language users or generated by a large language model. The implementation presented here is preliminary in nature and requires further calibration and empirical validation. The main contribution of this article is the proposal of a general methodological framework for the quantitative study of formal adequacy in various communicative contexts.

title: From Arraignment to Resolution: Transformer Models of Court Cases
author: Kory Rosen, Aron Culotta
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23518v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The criminal legal system is composed of many complex decision points, such as which charges are pursued, how bond is determined, plea deal negotiations, and sentencing. Given the profound impact of such decisions, there is a growing need to increase the transparency within this system. While prior machine learning approaches have focused on modeling single decisions (e.g., recidivism), this paper proposes a transformer-based time series model to forecast the outcome of the next proceeding in a case (e.g., charges accepted, bond set, plea deal made, etc.). By modeling a case as an event sequence, we enable a more nuanced analysis to support better oversight and understanding of decision making. We conduct an empirical analysis of thousands of cases using a newly constructed dataset derived from publicly available court records of a mid-sized U.S. city. We fit models that combine textual data from clerk notes with structured information about the defendant, prior charges, and courtroom. Our transformer model achieves $.57$ micro-F1 on a 20-class multi-label task, a significant improvement over several baselines and comparable to a GRU trained on the same input. We demonstrate how the model can be used to provide insights into decision-making and help court observers identify emerging issues within the jurisdiction studied.

title: Dreaming Up Authors: Factual Prevalence and LLM Hallucinations in Academic Authorship Attribution
author: Sijia Zhong, Tamir Yirga, Yijia Ma, Thai Le, Yifan Hu
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23530v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely used for question answering but are prone to hallucinations, yet the underlying causes, particularly the role of factual prevalence in training data, remain underexplored. In this work, we study this through academic authorship attribution, hypothesizing that hallucinations are more likely for less prevalent papers. Using citation count as a proxy for factual prevalence, we curate a dataset of 1.92 million papers across eight scientific disciplines with stratified samples by citation level. Experiments on three state-of-the-art LLMs confirm our hypothesis, revealing a robust inverse relationship between hallucination rate and citation count across all models and disciplines, with hallucination rates exceeding 98% for rarely cited papers and falling below 37% for highly cited ones. Our in-depth analysis further shows that these failures primarily reflect retrieval limitations rather than knowledge absence, and hidden-state probing of open-source models shows that factual prevalence is encoded in pre-generation representations, providing convergent mechanistic evidence for the prevalence-hallucination relationship. The code and data are available at https://github.com/quinnzhong1/dreaming-up-authors.

title: Can LLMs Understand What They Predict? Evaluating Latent Causal Structure Inference in Financial Markets
author: Yixiang Zheng, Yuechen Jiang, Zhiwei Liu, Jimin Huang, Yuyan Wang, Sophia Ananiadou
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23533v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated through their ability to predict future outcomes, implicitly assuming that predictive success reflects an understanding of the underlying system. However, accurate predictions can often be achieved without recovering the latent mechanisms that generate observable outcomes. To examine this assumption, we introduce LUCID, a benchmark that evaluates whether models can infer latent market structures from event descriptions and historical financial observations. Models generate event-induced causal graphs representing inferred market structure and are evaluated through a reconstruction-based framework. Our evaluation of 6 open-weight and proprietary LLMs shows that adding their generated graphs generally reduces reconstruction quality compared with using historical observations alone, although a few metrics improve. These findings suggest that inferring informative, event-specific market structures from observable evidence remains challenging for the evaluated LLMs.

title: Language Models Make New Research Sound Old
author: Guy Zyskind
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23546v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Researchers are increasingly using large language models (LLMs) to validate research questions. We find that LLMs make open research questions sound partly studied and overstate what related papers establish. Models recognize most of these overstatements when asked to check the papers' full texts separately. On 40 questions drawn from newly accepted papers, GPT-6-Astra correctly judges 98% to be unstudied, but states that status plainly in only 8% of ordinary answers. All six frontier systems show reporting gaps of 30-90 percentage points. Across 22 models given identical papers, higher capability is associated with more accurate judgments and larger reporting gaps. This reporting failure is asymmetric: models correctly identify studied questions in 88-100% of ordinary answers when we supply the answering papers. To correct this, we build a fixed answer from each model's judgment and separate checks of cited papers. This raises Astra's clear reporting of open status from 8% to 95%, with improvements in all six systems. Finally, we predict reviewers' novelty grades by combining several models' written ratings with a rule learned from graded examples, reaching the performance range reported by Think-Probe-Respond. Unlike TPR, our approach needs no access to model weights or internal activations, so it also works with closed-weight frontier models.

title: FutureBench: A Renewable Framework for Evaluating Knowledge-Context Conflict in LLMs
author: Yi-Cheng Lai, Hen-Hsen Huang
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23601v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Asking a model to check retrieved text can also tell it which source to trust. We introduce FutureBench, a renewable framework for evaluating knowledge-context conflict using timestamped questions, controlled passage triplets, and no-context probes. Across 3,629 questions and six models, Verify (a prompt combining checking with passage priority) raises false-answer adoption in all five models tested on pre-cutoff events, mainly by displacing answers that were correct under Baseline, which allows both passage evidence and model knowledge. On post-cutoff events, only o4-mini increases adoption (+13.7 percentage points). A four-prompt comparison on 902 post-cutoff questions finds that passage priority without checking raises adoption, while moving to Verify lowers it in all five models. Adversarial-Aware, which warns of misleading passages and prioritizes model knowledge, restores 82.5-98.9% of displaced pre-cutoff answers with under one point of change in true-passage accuracy. FutureBench supports repeated evaluation on fixed cohorts and extension to new events as models change.

title: Localizing Text Anonymization for Trustworthy AI: Extending RAT-Bench to Malaysian Microdata and PII
author: David Hong Liang Chew, Zexi Yao, Nata\v{s}a Kr\v{c}o, Matthieu Meeus, Waqas Khalid Obeidy, Yves-Alexandre de Montjoye
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23704v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As governments and organizations adopt foundation models for public services and workplace productivity, sensitive citizen, employee, and administrative text may enter LLM workflows through inference, retrieval, fine-tuning, or local model development. We examine whether text anonymizers transfer to new deployment settings by extending RAT-Bench to Malaysia using local microdata, Malaysian PII formats, and culturally grounded transcripts in Malaysian English and Bahasa Malaysia. We evaluate NER- and LLM-based anonymizers using an LLM attacker that infers attributes from anonymized text, measuring both re-identification success and text utility. Across Malaysian English and Bahasa Malaysia, the two LLM anonymizers provide the strongest explicit privacy-utility trade-offs, reducing Easy/Hard re-identification risk to 23-29% while preserving BLEU scores of 0.77-0.94. Non-LLM tools show sharper failure modes, either preserving utility while leaving high residual risk or reducing risk through severe over-redaction, especially in Bahasa Malaysia. These findings suggest that anonymizers should be evaluated against deployment-relevant languages, identifier formats, and cultural contexts before being relied on in public-sector, workplace, or local AI pipelines.

title: Beyond Replacement: Levenshtein Editing for Diffusion Language Models
author: Shuaidi Wang, Zhuocheng Gong, Xuejie Liu, Jianguo Li, Yu Zhang
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23750v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) offer a flexible alternative to autoregressive models, enabling any-order infilling. While most existing decoding methods treat decoded tokens as fixed, some recent models allow previously decoded tokens to be revised only by replacing them with alternative tokens, a paradigm we refer to as replacement-only editing (ROE). Although ROE can correct individual tokens, it is inefficient for sequence shifts caused by missing or extra tokens and struggles when errors occur across many positions. To address these limitations, we propose LED (Levenshtein Editing for Diffusion Language Models), a post-training framework that extends ROE with insertion and deletion, enabling Levenshtein-style refinement of generated sequences. It uses two training designs. First, it reconstructs edit supervision on the fly during supervised fine-tuning using longest-common-subsequence alignment, enabling insertion and deletion learning without manually annotated labels. Second, it adopts multi-stage training, where the state from one stage becomes the input to the next, exposing the model to its earlier errors and enabling it to correct them. When applied to the 16B-parameter LLaDA2.1-Mini Base, LED raises the average score across twelve benchmarks from 54.86 to 57.10 under confidence-guided decoding while increasing tokens per forward from 6.14 to 7.05, whereas under confidence-free decoding it raises the average score from 27.52 to 47.19. We further show that LED achieves higher pass@k at large k than thresholded decoding without editing, demonstrating improved generation diversity and revealing the diversity potential of DLMs without confidence guidance. LED also improves robustness to large block sizes, raising the average score from 36.97 to 51.34 at block size 128. Together, these results suggest that LED supports more robust self-correction in DLMs.

title: NarrowSpec: Draft Hidden Width Need Not Match the Target in Speculative Decoding
author: Alagappan Valliappan, Ankit More, Dheevatsa Mudigere, Jatin Mitra
contentSnippet: arXiv:2611.23835v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speculative decoding is widely used to speed up generation in large language models (LLMs), with a small draft model proposing tokens that one forward pass of the target model verifies. Draft models that read the target's hidden states, such as DFlash and EAGLE-3, typically inherit the target's hidden width. We show that the draft's whole residual stream can run at half or a quarter of that width while largely preserving acceptance. For DFlash, which borrows the target's vocabulary projection, the trained output adapter folds into it, giving one narrower projection with logits unchanged up to floating-point rounding. We test two drafter families, DFlash and EAGLE-3, on two targets, Qwen3-8B (NVFP4) and GPT-OSS-20B (MXFP4), in SGLang on a B200 and a DGX Spark (GB10). At batch size 1 and temperature 0, narrowing the draft to half or a quarter width speeds up end-to-end decoding by 1.06-1.12x on B200 and 1.13-1.44x on GB10. The speedup holds at larger batch sizes. From batch 32 to the largest batch each GPU fits, narrowing reaches up to 1.21x on both GPUs, and no narrow draft is slower than full width.
